summary: A large evergreen tree native to humid uplands on Madeira and the Canary Islands. It has been introduced to several nearby Azorean islands and is threatened by habitat loss.

A succulent flowering plant endemic to the Canary Islands, the candle-plant has jointed branches resembling rows of sausages. Thick elongated leaves cluster at branch tips and fall at the start of the dry season, while fragrant grey-white flowers may appear from March through October.

A succulent shrub endemic to the Canary Islands, it grows in a narrow coastal belt. Its fleshy four- or five-sided trunks resemble cacti and bear spines instead of leaves; it also produces reddish-green flowers and poisonous latex.
A flowering plant endemic to the Drakensberg in Southern Africa. It grows in moist grassland and on rocky slopes, and both of its subspecies are classified as least concern.

A low-branching evergreen tropical shrub native to tropical South America. Its leaves close and droop from dusk until morning, while its showy powder-puff flower heads gain their colour from numerous long stamens that are white below and pink above.

A herbaceous perennial whose native range depends on classification: it is treated either as widespread around the Mediterranean or native only to the Levant. It forms a ground-level leaf rosette around a large, sometimes human-shaped taproot, with usually purple flowers and yellow or orange berries. The root and leaves are poisonous.
edibilityNote: The root and leaves are poisonous; reported consumption has caused severe atropine-like symptoms, including hallucinations and rapid heartbeat.

summary: A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It parasitises the roots of Cistus albidus, with its vegetative body hidden inside the host as filaments. It is rare in Portugal, where widely scattered populations occur in dry scrub and open woodland.

Perennial herb native to the Spanish Mediterranean coast. Its varieties differ in silkiness and Mediterranean distribution, while the plant bears yellow flowers and fleshy leaflets. It grows in habitats ranging from sand to heavy saline soils.

Cactus-like succulent tree native to central India, Odisha and southern India’s Deccan. It has spreading, nearly five-sided branches, thorns and thick, spoon-shaped leaves. The leaves are eaten raw or cooked, including boiled with syrup or chopped as stuffing in parts of the Philippines, while the latex is irritating and toxic.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw or cooked, including boiled with syrup, made into sweets or used as stuffing in parts of the Philippines.

summary: Subtropical succulent tree native to Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Myanmar. Its thick branches bear clusters of sharp spines and fleshy leaves, with reddish flower-like structures grouped near the branch ends.

A shrub native to Morocco’s Atlas Mountain slopes, resin spurge forms broad, cushion-shaped clumps. Its upright, cactus-like succulent stems are four-angled and lined with short, sharp pairs of spines.
A shrub or thick-trunked tree native to southern Africa. Its short, horizontal branches form rosettes at the top of the main trunk and are succulent and triangular in cross-section.

Succulent shrub native to Mozambique, Eswatini and parts of South Africa. It has deeply segmented, three-angled stems with pairs of bull-horn-like spines, and small leaves that later fall off. Its showy fruit pops open when ripe.

A small, branching flowering plant endemic to Portugal’s Berlengas archipelago, it grows in open areas near coastal cliffs. Its yellow flowers appear between March and July, and the species is endangered.

summary: A perennial flowering plant endemic to western Iberia, including Portugal, Galicia and the Sierra Morena; one subspecies is native to the Berlengas archipelago. It generally has several low or rising stems, rosette-forming basal leaves and loose clusters of hairy, funnel-shaped flowers.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it occurs in mainland Portugal. It is protected under Annex V of the Habitats Directive.
Herbaceous perennial native to northwestern Spain and western Portugal. Its glossy dark-green foliage and hollow stems smell faintly of aniseed, while its pale flowers form broad, flat clusters.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A deciduous tree native to eastern China, Taiwan and Japan, it usually has glossy, three-lobed leaves, though unlobed leaves sometimes occur. Its paired winged seeds point forward and often overlap.

A flowering shrub or small tree endemic to the Andes from Colombia to northern Chile, red angel's trumpet has hanging, trumpet-shaped flowers in vivid red, yellow, orange and green. All parts are poisonous.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous and contain tropane alkaloids in varying proportions.

summary: A shrub or small tree native from Uganda to South Africa, forest num-num grows in woodland and forest. It has fragrant white flowers and fruit that turns red when ripe.

An evergreen tree native to low-elevation Himalayan woodlands in China, India, Pakistan, Nepal and Bhutan, it has grey-green leaves with pale, fuzzy undersides. White bracts surround its small greenish flowers, while several fruits fuse into a red body that is edible but usually bitter.
edibilityNote: The fused red fruit is edible but usually bitter.

summary: An evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub native to mountains, mixed forests and open places in western China, willow-leaved cotoneaster has arching branches and narrow, willow-like leaves with grey hairs beneath. Its small red fruits ripen in autumn and can persist into winter.

A deciduous shrub native to Japan, it is common throughout the country on forest edges and cliffs. It has opposite, thick, toothed leaves and flowers from May to July in Japan; a double-flowered form is popular in gardens.
Flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and present in mainland Portugal. It is protected under Portuguese or European legislation through Annexes II and IV of the Habitats Directive.
A flowering grass endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It is protected under Portuguese or European legislation, including Annexes II and IV of the Habitats Directive.
A flowering plant whose two listed subspecies are endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. Both grow on coastal dunes and sands, including primary dunes and hollows between dunes.
A flowering plant whose two listed varieties are native to mainland Portugal. It grows on coastal sands, mainly secondary dunes and sometimes ancient dunes.

An often-climbing shrub occurring around the Mediterranean except France, and on Madeira and the Canary Islands. It has glossy dark-green, toothed leaves, white or pale lilac flowers, and black fruit. It grows in scrub and evergreen woodland, especially near coasts, and in Portugal also occupies limestone rock crevices and scree.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Flowering plant whose subspecies have different documented origins: subsp. cabezudoi is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, while subsp. grandiflorus is native to mainland Portugal.
A flowering grass native to mainland Portugal. It grows in ponds and lagoons in both mountain and lowland areas.

A perennial, wintergreen aquatic plant native to temperate Europe, especially southern and western Europe. It roots in shallow water and bears broad floating leaves alongside finely divided, hairlike submerged leaves. Its flowers are pure white, and the plant is poisonous.
edibilityNote: The plant is poisonous when eaten.

sources.title: Ranunculus ololeucos J.Lloyd
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to the central and southern coast of mainland Portugal. It is an uncommon plant of coastal sands and secondary dunes, particularly near limestone areas or on lime-rich sandstone sands. It is protected under Annexes II and IV of the Habitats Directive.
A flowering plant found in the southern Iberian Peninsula, including mainland Portugal but not the Azores or Madeira. It favours uncultivated and disturbed ground and flowers from April to September.
A flowering wetland plant native to mainland Portugal and the Azores.
Annual herb native to the western Mediterranean Basin. It has a self-supporting growth form and flowers visited by several kinds of flies and a butterfly.

Flowering plant whose two listed subspecies are native to mainland Portugal. Unlike the marsh thistle used for comparison, it has well-developed stem leaves rather than especially developed basal leaves.
An aquatic rush native to the Mediterranean. In Portugal, it inhabits seasonally flooded meadows around ponds, reservoirs, lagoons and waterways.
A flowering plant endemic to mainland Portugal. It grows in clearings among coastal dune scrub, between dunes and sometimes beneath open pine woodland.

An annual plant native to southwestern Europe and Morocco, French groundsel is widespread across southern France and the Iberian Peninsula. It colonizes isolated, harsh habitats such as deserts, steppes, dry shrublands and salty coastal plains.
A climbing plant of unspecified native origin, Mediterranean asparagus is visited by Western honey bees and several kinds of flies and bees.

A deciduous shrub native to inland Portugal and central-western to southwestern Spain. It branches densely from the base and has spiny stems; male flowers are upright or spreading, while female flowers are somewhat hanging.
An Iberian-endemic flowering plant. It grows on stony ground, rock faces and fissures, walls, scree and sometimes roadsides, avoiding lime-rich ground.
Flowering plant; the subspecies Bufonia macropetala subsp. willkommiana is native to mainland Portugal.
An Iberian-endemic flowering plant. In Portugal, it grows in dry meadows, pastures and open scrub clearings on acidic ground.

A flowering plant whose listed subspecies are native to mainland Portugal. The typical subspecies grows in dry, sandy scrub clearings, pinewoods, cork-oak woodland and pasture; subspecies tuberculata occurs on acidic coastal sands beneath pine and cork-oak woodland.

Perennial flowering herb found in southwestern Europe and North Africa; the variety represented in Portugal is endemic to mainland Portugal. A 1913 account describes large, nearly spherical clusters with up to 50 or more flowers, blooming from June to September in wet places and ditches in central and southern Portugal. The species is classed as Near Threatened.
An erect deciduous shrub native to central and southern Europe and southwestern Asia. Its narrow grey-green leaves turn yellow in autumn, while green catkins appear with the new leaves in spring.

A perennial flowering rush native to Europe and southwest Asia, including the British Isles, great woodrush forms clumps of glossy, bright green leaves that stay greenish through winter. Scattered white hairs along the leaf edges help distinguish it from similar plants, and its tiny chestnut-brown flowers appear from mid-spring to summer.
A highly branched shrub found across much of the Iberian Peninsula, with clusters of yellow flowers from May to July. It favours dry, acidic, nutrient-poor soils in woodland clearings and heathland.
An Iberian-endemic flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in meadows beside waterways, along riverside woodland edges and on damp, shaded banks, usually over acidic sand or shale.
An Iberian-endemic flowering plant. It grows in scrub along woodland edges and in open plantations, favouring rocky shale or granite and occurring rarely on limestone.
A perennial herb native to mainland Portugal. It has yellow flower heads on upright, sometimes hollow stems and grows in damp meadows, pastures, woodland edges and deciduous woods.

sources.title: Crepis lampsanoides (Gouan) Tausch
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An evergreen dwarf shrub native to eastern England, France, Spain and Portugal, dwarf gorse is restricted to lowland heathland. It forms low bushes among heather, with small scales or spines instead of typical leaves and soft, crowded green spines on its shoots. Yellow flowers appear mainly in late summer and autumn, rarely before July.
Flowering plant native exclusively to the Iberian Peninsula. It belongs to the legume family and occurs in mainland Portugal.

A perennial flowering plant whose native origin is not specified. Its spreading branches form mats, with narrow rolled-edged leaves and whitish flowers; it inhabits maritime sands, shingle and dry salt marshes.
A flowering wetland perennial native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia, tubular water-dropwort has brittle, inflated hollow stems and forms distinctive pink fruiting balls after flowering.
edibilityNote: In parts of southern Italy and Turkey, the basal leaves have traditionally been cooked as a meal.

summary: An aquatic flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in shallow, temperate standing water, including lakes, ponds, pools and quiet backwaters, generally where the water is nutrient-rich and neutral.
Tussock-forming perennial sedge native to the Mediterranean. It favours wet, non-saline bogs, ditches and marshes, and bears unusually long female flower spikes.
A flowering plant endemic to Portugal’s central-west limestone region. It has fleshy, scalloped leaves, white flowers and dense glandular hairs, and grows mainly in limestone rock crevices and walls.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Saxifraga cintrana
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A perennial flowering plant native to Brazil, purple allamanda is grown as an ornamental and bears purple, bell-shaped flowers. Its stems can yield very strong, silky white fibre after chemical treatment.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in dry, often stony clearings among open scrub, thickets and holm-oak woods, especially on limestone, gypsum or clay soils.

sources.title: Cleonia lusitanica (L.) L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual native to the Mediterranean, Middle East, India, Pakistan and Central Asia. Its woolly growth bears conspicuous three-part fruits that twist open and propel their seeds. Fruit-coat and leaf-sap extracts yielded a blue-purple dye historically used in manuscripts and as a food colorant, although consuming the plant may cause digestive illness.
edibilityNote: Fruit-coat or leaf-sap colorant was used in Dutch cheese and liquors, although consuming the plant may cause digestive illness.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It is found in sparse grasslands and meadows on dry, acidic, sandy or stony ground.

Evergreen tree endemic to New Zealand, pūriri has glossy leaves usually divided into five leaflets and large tubular flowers ranging from pink or red to occasional white. Some flowers and ripe fruit occur year-round, with flowering heaviest in winter and fruit more common in summer.
edibilityNote: The bitter fruit is not a traditional Māori food.

summary: A small evergreen tree endemic to Macaronesia, it is found in the Azores, Madeira and the Canary Islands and is an important part of high-altitude laurel forest. It has leathery dark-green leaves, white to pink flowers and red toxic berries.
edibilityNote: The red berries are toxic.

summary: A spurge-family plant native to southern Africa.

An agave native to the Mexican states of Hidalgo, Tamaulipas and San Luis Potosí, it forms clusters of fleshy blue-green to yellow-green leaves with relatively soft brown spines. Its tall flowering stalk bears green flowers packed closely against the stem in a narrow column.
A succulent subshrub or shrub native from Mali to Djibouti, growing mainly in seasonally dry tropical habitats.

sources.title: Aloe macrocarpa Tod. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: An evergreen tree native to Australia, with rough bark, waxy leaves and flushes of pink new growth. Its cream-white flowers are followed in winter by edible berries ranging from white to maroon.
edibilityNote: An 1889 account says Aboriginal people and children ate the mildly acidic fruit and called it wholesome; it has also been described as rather tasteless.

summary: A flowering plant native only to coastal New South Wales near Sydney. Its rosette of long, sword-shaped leaves produces a towering stalk topped with bright red, trumpet-shaped flowers visited by bees and nectar-feeding birds.
edibilityNote: Aboriginal people roasted young stems for eating and roasted roots to make a kind of cake.

summary: An annual herb with native subspecies in mainland Portugal and Madeira. It commonly branches from the base, bears white or lilac flowers, and grows in dry, stony grasslands, scrub clearings and beside temporary waterways.

sources.title: Convolvulus siculus L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An aquatic or emergent flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It inhabits very wet, acidic places such as pools, lakes, springs, streams and peat bogs.

A bulbous herbaceous perennial native across much of Europe, northern Africa and western Asia. Its tall stems carry tightly packed, spherical or egg-shaped heads containing many reddish-purple flowers; small bulblets and occasional bulbils can make it potentially invasive in gardens.
A wild onion native to Spain, Portugal and Morocco. Its flowers are yellow, and in Portugal it grows in generally damp perennial meadows within alder, oak and pine woods.

sources.title: Allium scorzonerifolium Desf. ex Redouté
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). English Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/c3kkgh accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A bulb-forming perennial herb found across southern and central Europe. It bears rounded clusters of white, bell-shaped flowers with stamens projecting beyond the petals.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A perennial herb recorded in western Iberia and western France. It grows in peat bogs, wet meadows and riverside forests on acidic soils, flowering from September to October and fruiting in November.

A stemless perennial flowering plant native to the western Mediterranean Basin, particularly the Iberian Peninsula and northwestern Maghreb. Its leaves rise directly from a tuber, while its flower cluster is enclosed by a purple-spotted tube with a curved, forward-tilting helmet shape.

A bulbous perennial bluebell endemic to the northwestern Iberian Peninsula. It grows chiefly in shady woodland and produces clusters of pale-blue spring flowers, usually in March and April but sometimes as late as June in upland areas.

A bulbous perennial strictly endemic to the western and central-western Iberian Peninsula. Its narrow leaves and upright flower stalk emerge from a single underground bulb. Between March and July it typically bears white flowers, often with a green stripe, in rocky crevices, mountain scrub and other open ground on acidic soils.

A bulbous perennial endemic to mountains of northern Portugal, southern Galicia and the westernmost Spanish Central System, paradise lily grows sporadically in cool, shady woods. It bears loose clusters of white, broadly bell-shaped or star-shaped flowers in spring.

A flowering plant of unspecified overall native origin, it has two documented subspecies in mainland Portugal. The typical subspecies is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, while subspecies alpestris is endemic to mainland Portugal.
A flowering plant native across Europe to western Siberia and Turkey.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, Myosotis welwitschii belongs to the borage family. It is protected under Portuguese or European Community law, including Annexes II and IV of the Habitats Directive.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows on rocky ground and in woodland or scrub clearings, favouring acidic soils in mountain areas.
Flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in rock crevices and open grassland on acidic, stony soils.
Flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It inhabits acidic sandy grassland, rock crevices and rocky slopes, and sometimes occurs on dunes.

A sedge native to Atlantic Europe from Fennoscandia to the Iberian Peninsula, it grows in damp, acidic habitats such as heaths and moorland. Its fruiting structures bear two conspicuous green veins, while aging leaves develop wine-red patches.
Sedge native to the lowlands of Western and Central Europe, where it grows in moist, shady places, particularly alder–ash woodland. Tiny red dots on its utricles distinguish it from similar species.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It usually grows in shade beneath woodland or on rocky outcrops and is not restricted to a particular substrate.

Deciduous fern endemic to Macaronesia and the Iberian Peninsula. It has thick, scaly creeping stems and broad, finely divided fronds, and grows on tree trunks, branches and mossy rocks in cool, humid places influenced by the ocean.

Large herbaceous flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows mainly in hay meadows and along stream banks in the mountains of northern Portugal, where it is considered Vulnerable, with only seven known locations and an estimated population of fewer than 2,500 mature plants.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: Flowering plant native to Europe. It is less acrid than other spurges, while the purple-leaved cultivar 'Chameleon' is the form most commonly planted in gardens.

sources.title: Euphorbia dulcis L.
sources.attribution: Info Flora, plazi (2021). Info Flora Schweiz - Euphorbiaceae. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/2m8qx3 accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.
Flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in scrub on cleared or neglected land, field edges, slopes and roadsides, mainly on disturbed acidic soils in Atlantic-influenced areas.

A herbaceous perennial native to western Europe and northern Africa. It has characteristically wavy-edged leaves, winged stems with black glands, and bright-yellow flowers whose petals are tinged red on the back.
Iris native to Europe, mainly Spain and Portugal. It normally carries one blue-purple or deep-purple flower per stem in June, marked by a yellow or orange beard.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It occurs in generally moist grassland and scrub, cultivated fields and roadsides, preferring stony, silica-rich soils.

sources.title: Malva tournefortiana L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Woody flowering subshrub native to mainland Portugal. It has slender branches, small deciduous leaves and blue flowers in clusters near the upper branches, flowering from February to June.
Flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in dry grassland, pine clearings and open scrub, usually on dry, stony, silica-rich soils.
Flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It occurs in clearings among heathland and pine woods on silica-rich ground.

A meadow-rue native to Portugal and Spain on the Iberian Peninsula and to Morocco and Algeria in northwestern Africa. It belongs to the Betic-Rifan flora shared by southern Spain and northern Morocco.

Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal but introduced in the Azores and Madeira. It frequents fallow fields, pasture, scrub clearings and slopes, often on moist, acidic sandy soils enriched by human or animal activity.

A rare wild pear shrub or small deciduous tree of Atlantic western Europe, occurring in France, Spain and Portugal, with a small British presence believed to be anciently introduced. It grows in hedgerows and woodland edges and bears pale cream blossom tinged pink, with an unpleasant smell.

A perennial herb found in Western Europe, meadow bastard toadflax has narrow, three-veined leaves arranged alternately on upright stems. Its tube-shaped flowers bloom in June and July, with petal tips rolling inward as the fruit develops.

A perennial plant of unstated native origin, commonly found in Western Europe and North Africa beside rivers, ponds and other damp places. Its greenish-purple square stems have conspicuous corner wings, and it bears small, rounded maroon-brown flowers.

A flowering plant with a native range described as oceanic western Europe, from the British Isles and Atlantic France to northwestern Spain and Portugal near the Tagus. Its single flowers range from milky violet to greyish pink, with deep purple veins on the lower petal and green spurs behind.
Fern native to mainland Portugal and the Azores and Madeira archipelagos. It favors rocky habitats and also occurs elsewhere in Europe, Africa, and Central and South America.

Small salt-tolerant shrub found mainly along Mediterranean coasts and northward along Atlantic coasts to southeastern England; its native origin is not explicitly stated. Its appearance varies widely, and it grows in salt flats, salt marshes and similar dry or semi-dry salty habitats.
A daffodil native to Spain, Portugal and Morocco. It has solitary yellow flowers that range from horizontal to upright and grows on rocky cliffs, dunes and meadows in either lime-rich or acidic soil.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows on coastal sandy soils in pine woods and clearings among dune scrub.
A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, sea pearlwort is found throughout Europe, Southwest Asia, North Africa, the Canary Islands and the Azores.

An annual flowering herb native to mainland Portugal. In Portugal, it grows in grasslands on sand and acidic ground; its flowers are reported as usually four-parted, though this feature needs confirmation.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. In Portugal, it grows on coastal sands, rocks and cliffs, sometimes in grassland on stabilized dunes.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, but introduced in the Azores. It belongs to the pea family.

An annual herb whose native origin is not stated. It is extremely short-stemmed, with upright three-part leaves and small white flower clusters tucked into the leaf axils. Its heavy fruits press the clusters to the ground, where the seeds germinate.

sources.title: Trifolium suffocatum L.
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A parasitic flowering plant native to the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa, from the Canary Islands and Madeira to Morocco and Algeria. In Portugal, it grows in disturbed grassy or agricultural places and parasitizes herbs, mainly daisies and their relatives; in Tunisia it was collected on Calendula suffruticosa.

sources.attribution: Mokni R E, Domina G, Barone G, felipe (2023). New records of the genus Orobanche L. (Orobanchaceae) to the Tunisian flora with lectotypification of the name O. rapum-genistae Thuill.. Adansonia. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/k8tygy accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual grass native to parts of Europe, western Asia and North Africa. It has simple, broad leaves and a self-supporting growth form.

An annual herb native to the Azores and found throughout much of the Mediterranean. Its upright stems bear sparse stinging hairs, coarse-toothed leaves and tail-like male flower spikes near the top. In Sicily, its cooked leaves are eaten as a spinach-like vegetable or in soup.
edibilityNote: In Sicily, cooked leaves are eaten as nettle spinach or soup; the plant was also eaten in 19th-century Greece.

sources.title: Urtica membranacea Poir.
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A bulbous plant endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula. In mainland Portugal it occurs only in the Algarve, on rocky limestone ground and outcrops, usually in small scattered groups. There it was assessed as Vulnerable, with fewer than 10,000 mature plants estimated and a continuing national decline inferred.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A tiny fern whose native origin is not stated in the supplied information. Its short fronds are densely hairy and gland-bearing, and it produces spores through most of the year. During hot, dry summers its fronds dehydrate and appear dead, then quickly become green again after autumn rain.
A flowering plant native to southern Europe and North Africa.

A shrub whose native origin is not stated. It has slender green stems and sheds its leaves in hot weather, leaving a rush-like outline; clusters of yellow flowers appear in spring and summer. It grows in dry, sunny scrub on stony or sandy ground, especially limestone, and is described as toxic.
edibilityNote: Described as toxic; the source does not specify a plant part or preparation.

sources.title: Coronilla juncea L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant with no species-wide native origin stated. Its two listed Portuguese subspecies, subsp. algarbiensis and subsp. hirsuta, are endemic to the Iberian Peninsula.
A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, it includes subsp. haenseleri, which is present in mainland Portugal and endemic to the Iberian Peninsula.

An obligate parasitic plant native to many areas around the Mediterranean, Cytinus hypocistis lives inside the roots of rock-roses. It has no chlorophyll, external roots, leaves or stems; only its sweet-smelling flowers emerge during the reproductive season.
A shrub endemic to the central and western Iberian Peninsula, sage-leaved willow has greyish, densely hairy twigs. Its whitish leaves have a soft covering of hairs underneath.
Creeping perennial herb endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in very wet soil or underwater and has leaves divided into four fan-shaped parts, though it is not a true clover.

A robust perennial herb whose native origin is not stated. It has softly hairy, grooved stems that branch toward the top and a strong, distinctive coumarin smell. It occurs in the southwestern and central Mediterranean, including North Africa, in dry places, roadsides and waste ground.

An annual oilseed plant native to the Mediterranean. Its white, sometimes pink flowers are followed by unusually smooth, nearly spherical upper fruit sections. It grows in sheltered, reliably moist rock crevices on either siliceous or limestone ground.

A tiny annual flowering plant whose native origin is not stated. It has narrow, fleshy, often reddish leaves and pink flowers, and can form loose patches. In Portugal, it favors damp sandy places and temporarily flooded margins of rivers, marshes, pools and other hollows.

sources.title: Crassula vaillantii (Willd.) Roth
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual flowering herb native to southern Europe and North Africa, it has leaves divided like the fingers of a hand. Its pistil sits on a long stalk-like section above the stamens, and it flowers from April to August.

A shrub native to the southern Iberian Peninsula, restricted to a small area of southeastern Portugal and southwestern Spain. It mostly grows in metal-contaminated soils, often around mines; in Portugal it is documented only near Mina de São Domingos, beside acidic lagoons and mine waste.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Erica andevalensis
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: An annual herb of unstated native origin, it occurs across western North Africa, Europe and western Asia. It is light green and bristly-haired, with reduced red petals, and often grows in wet, open river-valley sites, especially on sandy soil.

A parasitic plant native to Europe, greater broomrape lacks chlorophyll and depends entirely on other plants for nutrients. It usually grows on the roots of common broom or European gorse and has a honey-brown, downy stem that persists as a dark brown spike after flowering.
An annual flowering herb native to mainland Portugal and Madeira. It grows as a field weed in fallow ground and cultivated fields, generally on alkaline soils.
An annual herb native to southern Europe, Lamium bifidum has upright or trailing stems. It bears dense groups of white flowers with a deeply split lower petal, and some flowers remain closed.

Seaweed of unstated native origin, with its type locality at Helgoland, Germany. Its light-green, hollow tubular fronds grow in clusters from a disc-like cushion. It occurs on rocks, barnacles, driftwood and even other algae in sheltered areas.

Fast-growing shrub native to Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay. It produces abundant blue-purple flowers with yellow centres, followed by colourful berries. All parts are considered toxic to humans.
edibilityNote: All parts are considered toxic to humans; the attractive fruit may be poisonous and is not recommended for consumption.

summary: Evergreen woody climber native to Madagascar. It bears clusters of waxy, star-shaped white flowers with an intense fragrance, alongside glossy dark-green leaves.

Evergreen Australian shrub native from near Bilpin in New South Wales north to Queensland, usually in coastal wet forests and rainforests. It has long, narrow leaves, mauve flower clusters and distinctive purple-to-black fruit—the only Australian Cordyline reported to have black fruit.
A flowering plant native to China, Mongolia and Korea. Its ‘Canary Bird’ cultivar has received the Royal Horticultural Society’s Award of Garden Merit.

A small- to medium-sized tree endemic to south-eastern continental Australia, it has mostly smooth white, yellow or bluish-grey bark. Its white, red or pink flowers develop from distinctive groups of three buds, followed by woody cylindrical, barrel-shaped or rounded fruit.
A tree endemic to eastern Australia. It has rough, stringy bark, curved lance-shaped adult leaves, clusters of white flowers, and woody rounded fruit; it can regrow from buds after bushfire.

A large, single-stemmed aloe of Southern Africa, ranging from the Johannesburg area through parts of Botswana, Zimbabwe, Malawi, Eswatini and Mozambique. It bears a robust crown of stiff grey-green leaves, usually with many short spines. Its winter flower clusters typically branch horizontally and range from yellow through orange to bright red.
An evergreen shrub native to western Hubei, China. Its young branches bear yellow spines, while its yellow flowers are followed by egg-shaped blue berries with a white waxy coating.

A fig tree native to Africa south of the Sahel and north of the Tropic of Capricorn, excluding central-west rainforest areas, the sycamore fig has a dense, spreading crown and green-yellow to orange bark that peels away in papery strips. Depending on the variety, it fruits year-round from April or later, producing thick clusters of edible figs that ripen yellow or red.
edibilityNote: The fruit is edible; fruiting begins in April or later depending on variety and may continue year-round.

summary: A small tree found across parts of Africa, India and Sri Lanka. It has drooping slender branches and bell-shaped yellow flowers marked with dark maroon at the base.

A flowering shrub native to mountains from Eritrea to South Africa, Rotheca myricoides has asymmetrical flowers that vary from green and blue to mauve, white and blue. Its often velvety leaves release an unpleasant scent when crushed.

A prickly evergreen shrub with a pantropical range, especially in dry forests, foothills and scrub. It bears white flowers followed by fruit from April. Various parts, especially flowers and fruit, are reported as used either for food or traditional medicine.
edibilityNote: Various parts, especially flowers and fruit, are reported as used either as food or in traditional medicine.

summary: A perennial orchid with a Mediterranean-Atlantic distribution from Charente through south-central Europe and the Mediterranean Basin to Cyprus. Its variable purple-red flowers form a helmet above a large, hairy lip and produce no nectar; their tubes instead shelter insect pollinators.
A flowering plant in the cabbage family, represented in mainland Portugal by two native subspecies. One of these, subspecies vicentina, is found naturally only in that region.

A fern native to Europe, it has delicate, highly divided fronds with translucent leaves growing from a creeping rhizome. Its unusual life cycle includes a perennial phase that reproduces vegetatively and tolerates darker, drier habitats than the frond-bearing form.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Vandenboschia speciosa
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A perennial herb native to Europe, it forms dense tufts. Its blue flowers cluster in compact heads on mostly leafless upper stems, and it inhabits meadows, open woodland, roadsides and rocky places.

sources.title: Jasione laevis Lam.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A small shrubby tree native to the Mediterranean region, spiny broom has very spiny branches and bright yellow flowers from January through April. Its florets were used in antiquity to flavor sesame oil and are still used by local Arabs to flavor butter.
edibilityNote: The florets historically flavored sesame oil and are still used locally to flavor butter.

summary: A perennial or biennial herb native to southern Europe. It has short, stiff hairs, finely divided stem leaves and blue-violet flower heads whose calyx bristles are usually absent or exceptionally few and short.

sources.title: Scabiosa triandra L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A thistle endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. Its whitish-haired stems have spiny wings, while the large divided leaves bear long spines; clustered flower heads are purple, or very rarely white.
Grass endemic to mainland Portugal. It grows in high-mountain meadows and is currently known only from Serra da Estrela; records suggesting a wider historical range still require confirmation.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Festuca henriquesii
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A thorny shrub native to Europe and also found in northwestern Morocco. It grows mainly beneath cork oaks and other oaks on acidic ground, and has three-part leaves and loose flower clusters. It flowers and fruits from April to June.
Flowering plant in the pea family; its subspecies Genista tournefortii subsp. tournefortii is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and occurs in mainland Portugal.

A sub-succulent shrub endemic to Portugal’s Arrábida Natural Park, it grows on south-facing limestone cliffs between Cabo Espichel and Sesimbra. It has green or slightly bluish leaves and yellowish-green or reddish fruit containing reddish-brown seeds.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Euphorbia pedroi
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A perennial subshrub of unstated native origin, it occurs in the Mediterranean region. Its lower stems are woody, its upper half branches, and it bears pink flower heads that become long-stalked as the fruit develops.

sources.title: Cheirolophus sempervirens (L.) Pomel
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, clasping-leaved jointed glasswort tolerates salty conditions. In a 2016–2019 mainland Portuguese assessment, it was confined to a tiny area between Faro and Olhão, with fewer than 2,500 mature plants estimated and was assessed as Critically Endangered.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Halopeplis amplexicaulis
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A bulb-forming herb endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, occurring in Portugal and southwestern Spain. It has narrow cylindrical leaves and dense spherical or hemispherical flower clusters, with purple outer flower parts and paler inner ones.

Bulbous perennial native to Portugal, Spain and Morocco, where it grows on dry sandy ground. It generally has three extremely narrow leaves per bulb. Its late-winter or early-spring flowers are usually white but may be pink-tinged or entirely pink.

A perennial bulbous flowering plant of unspecified native origin, it occurs in western Iberia and northwestern Morocco, mainly in open woods and pastures. It usually bears a single leaf and a small cluster of white flowers without conspicuous green stripes on their backs, flowering from February to March.
A herbaceous plant native to southern Spain and Morocco. It is densely covered with yellowish star-shaped hairs and grows in grassland on sandy soils; flowering and fruiting occur from April to June.

sources.title: Andryala arenaria (DC.) Boiss. & Reut.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant whose nominate subspecies is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and occurs in mainland Portugal.
An annual flowering herb native to mainland Portugal. It grows on coastal dunes in disturbed sandy soils and has lance-shaped to narrow oblong leaves with wavy, toothed edges.

sources.title: Hedypnois arenaria (Schousb.) DC.
sources.attribution: Kilian N (2024). Cichorieae Systematics Portal. Botanic Garden and Botanical Museum Berlin. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/gzcrwf accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A perennial succulent native to Kenya, it has a thick, fleshy underground stem and knobbly stems whose leaves usually form five spiral rows. It grows on steep, rocky grassland and volcanic slopes among lava rocks.

Flowering herbaceous perennial native to rocky hillsides, shrubland and woodland from south-central Turkey to the Levant. Its nodding flowers have strongly upswept petals and are sweetly scented in the wild, though cultivated forms have lost the scent. Palestinians use its leaves to make stuffed leaves, while its tuberous root is described as semi-poisonous.
edibilityNote: Palestinians use the leaves to make stuffed leaves; the tuberous root is described as semi-poisonous.

summary: An annual herb occurring across the Mediterranean region. Its parts smell of fennel, and its glandular flower heads bear yellow florets; in Portugal it grows beneath pine, cork oak and scrub on acidic, sometimes damp soils.

sources.title: Senecio lividus L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant represented in mainland Portugal by two documented subspecies. Subspecies contracta is native there, while subspecies welwitschii is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and also occurs in mainland Portugal.

A bulbous flowering plant from the western Mediterranean region, it grows in uncultivated fields, preferably on acidic soils. Its narrow leaves appear almost alongside lilac flowers, usually one and rarely two per bulb, from October to November.
A perennial herb endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa. It is hairless and many-stemmed, with leathery, toothed elliptical leaves; male and female flowers occur on separate plants.

An annual sand-loving legume recorded around Mediterranean and Macaronesian coasts. Its low, branching growth may be partly buried in sand, with slightly fleshy blue-green leaves and lemon-yellow flowers whose largest petal is hairy underneath.

sources.title: Ononis variegata Linnaeus 1753
sources.attribution: Jarvis C, admin (2007). Chapter 7: Linnaean Plant Names and their Types (part O). Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.291971 accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Flowering bush native to Mediterranean areas of Algeria, Morocco, Portugal, Spain, Egypt, the East Aegean Islands and Greece, bridal veil broom has been introduced elsewhere. Its seeds contain cytisine, a toxic alkaloid.

A perennial orchid centred on the western Mediterranean, also recorded in the Azores, northwestern Africa and as far east as southern Turkey. Its broad, purple, heart-shaped flower lip has two diverging ridges at the base, while the leaves and stem base are often reddish or violet-spotted.

sources.title: Serapias cordigera L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual grass recorded in southwestern Europe and North Africa. It has an open, delicate flower cluster with hair-thin branches and spikelet stalks conspicuously thickened at their tips, flowering in May.

An annual grass recorded along coasts of southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia. It grows on coastal sands and dunes, with stems that may be upright, rising or trailing and elongated spikelets that flower from April to June.

sources.title: Cutandia maritima (L.) Barbey
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering grass whose supplied sources do not establish an undisputed native origin. It grows in dry, warm meadows along the edges of scrub and thickets.

An autumn-flowering daffodil native to Portugal, Spain and Morocco; records farther east in the Mediterranean refer to other species. Its fragrant flowers have white tepals and one of the genus’s smallest coronas, which is yellow.

A perennial herb native to the Mediterranean region. Short, stiff hairs make it very rough to the touch, while its profusely branching stems often form a rounded outline topped by yellow flower clusters.

sources.title: Cachrys sicula Linnaeus 1762
sources.attribution: Jarvis C, admin (2007). Chapter 7: Linnaean Plant Names and their Types (part C). Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.291971 accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, Daucus crinitus belongs to the carrot family and has two Portuguese common names: cenoura-brava-de-crina and cenoura-de-folha-miúda.

Perennial herb native to parts of northern Africa and southern Europe. It has broad leaves and typically grows in garrigue and steppe. In Portugal, where it is currently known only from Algarve fallows on marly limestone soil, it was assessed as Critically Endangered.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Kundmannia sicula
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: An annual weed of the Mediterranean region. It has a strong smell, finely divided leaves and small clusters of yellow flowers; the leaves are eaten raw or cooked and used to flavour pickles.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw or cooked and used as an herb in the pickle industry.

summary: A Mediterranean herb that usually forms a very aromatic, greyish or green subshrub. It grows on brackish clay or sand in salt marshes, coastal sands and salt-tolerant scrub, flowering mainly from late summer into autumn.

sources.title: Artemisia caerulescens L.
sources.attribution: C. Benedi, A. Buira, E. Rico, M. B. Crespo, A. Quintanar, C. Aedo, S. Castroviejo, plazi (2019). Flora Iberica / Vol. XVI (III): Compositae (partim). Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/28egpw accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual herb, the cage thistle is self-supporting and has simple, broad leaves and dry fruit.

Annual flowering plant endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula. In mainland Portugal it occurs only near Castro Marim, mainly in meadows and fallow extensively farmed land, and was assessed as Endangered.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Picris willkommii
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: An annual herb found across southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia. Its succulent leaves accompany small clusters of yellow flowers, followed by curved pods divided into clearly marked segments.
A trailing plant of unstated native origin, with white, pea-shaped flowers marked by purple veins. Its small oval leaves are hairy underneath and smooth above.
An annual herb with no native origin stated, Sicilian melilot has a self-supporting form and broad, compound leaves.

An annual herb endemic to Iberia and the Maghreb. It has hairy, glandular stems and long-stalked flowers with a pink, reddish-veined upper petal and yellow lower petals, typically growing in scrub and grassland on loose acidic soils.
A flowering species represented in mainland Portugal by two subspecies native there. The subspecies gaditana is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula.

An upright tree or rounded shrub native to southwestern Western Australia, it has sharp, needle-shaped leaves. Its abundant white or cream flowers are sweetly scented and tipped with pink or brownish pollen, while its woody egg-shaped fruits end in two prominent horns.
A tuberous perennial herb endemic to Madeira, the Madeira orchid produces spikes of intense magenta-pink flowers in late spring.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and introduced in the Azores. It favours dry shrub openings, open cork or holm-oak woods, roadsides and secondary dunes, usually on siliceous ground or sand and only rarely on limestone.
An annual herb of the Mediterranean region of southern Europe. It has solitary orange-yellow flower heads and blooms from April to July, and it has become invasive in parts of southern South America.
A flowering species native to mainland Portugal and belonging to the daisy family.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it occurs in mainland Portugal.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows on sandy soil in clearings, roadsides and fallow ground, including both coastal and inland dunes.

Flowering plant native to Portugal and Spain, particularly near their coasts. Its populations have several different multiples of the basic chromosome set, the widest such series recorded in its genus.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It occurs in short-lived herb communities beneath scrub and woodland, favouring cool, shady places.
A low-growing flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It favours low scrub and slopes in dry, sunny, warm and rocky places, especially on limestone-derived ground.

sources.title: Fumana laevipes (L.) Spach
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A perennial rock-rose native to the western Mediterranean, it is often woody near the base and branches freely. Its simple leaves accompany loosely arranged flowers.
A wetland flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in damp dune hollows, peatlands, marshes and rice fields.
An annual flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in dry annual grasslands and scrub openings, especially on sandy, schist or quartz-rich soils.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows on coastal sandy soils, including secondary dunes, pinewood and broom-scrub openings, and roadsides.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It inhabits dry scrub and pinewood openings on acidic sandy soils.

An annual herb native to North Africa, southern Europe and western Asia as far as Iran, yellow milkvetch has compound, broad leaves. Its seed pods are edible, and its roasted seeds were used as a coffee substitute, especially when coffee was scarce in the 1800s.
edibilityNote: The seed pods are edible; roasted seeds were used as a coffee substitute, especially during coffee shortages in the 1800s.

summary: A trailing plant ranging from central and southern Portugal through southern Spain and Morocco to Senegal. It has hairy, sand-coloured stems, three spaced pea-like leaves and small yellow pea-like flowers above hairy forked bases. Its leaves range from smooth to hairy depending on location.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and restricted to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula and northwestern Morocco. In Portugal it is known only from mildly nutrient-enriched coastal sands on the Setúbal Peninsula, where habitat decline and a projected population decline contributed to its Endangered assessment.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Ononis cossoniana
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: Woody, upright perennial flowering plant native to southern Portugal and Spain. Its fleshy, oval, pale green leaves are furry underneath, and white, lilac or pink flowers grow on spikes protected by green bracts.

A semi-parasitic herb endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. Its self-pollinating flowers change from pale yellow through orange to reddish brown. It occurs in dry grassland, open woodland and disturbed ground on varied soils.

sources.title: Odontitella virgata (Link) Rothm.
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A chlorophyll-free parasitic plant ranging from the Arabian Peninsula and Syrian Desert across North Africa and southern Europe to Macaronesia. Its stout fleshy stems bear dense, bright yellow flowers, and it is eaten like asparagus.
edibilityNote: The plant is used as food and eaten like asparagus.

summary: A flowering plant whose two listed subspecies occur in mainland Portugal. Subspecies bipunctata is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, while subsp. glutinosa is described as endemic to mainland Portugal and receives legal protection there.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal but introduced to Madeira. It grows in annual grasslands, pastures, fallow ground, open scrub and pinewoods, usually on acidic soils.
Small shrub endemic to Sardinia, Corsica, Portugal and Spain. This rare coastal plant grows on sand dunes and beaches, producing pale pink flower heads on long stalks above pointed leaves.
A flowering species represented in mainland Portugal by two subspecies native there.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in grasslands, pastures and scrub openings on varied ground, with some preference for acidic soils.

A semi-parasitic plant found across parts of Africa, the Canary Islands and the southern Iberian Peninsula, African sandalwood has scented wood used to extract essential oil. It grows in rocky places and along dry-forest margins and is usually uncommon in any one location.

Flowering plant endemic to Portugal’s Madeira Archipelago. It is protected by Portuguese or European Community legislation, including Annex I of the Convention on European Wildlife and Natural Habitats.

A flowering plant endemic to Deserta Grande in Madeira, it faces imminent extinction. A 2021 study found only ten individuals, nine of them genetically identical, with feral-goat grazing identified as its main threat.
A biennial or perennial herb endemic to the Madeira Archipelago, Matthiola maderensis bears very fragrant terminal clusters of violet or purple flowers, which are rarely white.
Succulent-leaved subshrub endemic to the Azores and Madeira Islands. Its finely hairy leaves accompany swanlike flowers with red wings and yellow beaks, while green hairless seed pods stand upright.

Perennial woody shrub endemic to Madeira Island. Its flower heads combine reddish-purple disc flowers that turn yellow after opening with pinkish-white outer flowers. This rare plant grows on moist, rocky coastal slopes of Madeira and the Desertas Islands.

Flowering plant with two subspecies native only to Madeira’s Selvagens Islands, Lobularia canariensis belongs to the cabbage family. These subspecies, rosula-venti and succulenta, do not occur on Madeira Island, Porto Santo or the Desertas.

A perennial rosette plant of unspecified native origin, recorded from the Selvagens Islands. Its flat rosettes have rounded leaves that narrow sharply into long, stalk-like bases, and its flowers are usually six-parted.

sources.title: Monanthes lowei (Paiva) P.Pérez & Acebes
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to Fora Islet in the Savage Islands, Selvagens spurge grows in basalt crags sheltered from salty winds. It has been considered Critically Endangered because its population is highly restricted.
A flowering plant native to Madeira.
Compact woody flowering shrub endemic to Madeira. It has narrow, densely hairy silver-green leaves and pale blue to bluish-rose flowers gathered in egg-shaped clusters.
A woody perennial shrub endemic to Madeira. It is highly branched and may grow upright or along the ground, bearing flower heads with white outer petals and yellow centres from March to July.
A flowering plant in the pea family, reported from and native to Madeira.
An annual or biennial herb endemic to Madeira. Its erect stems often have a purple tinge and branch from the base, carrying up to five heads of yellow flowers.

sources.title: Crepis divaricata F.Schultz
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A shrubby succulent endemic to the Madeira archipelago. It is a flowering member of the spurge family, and its international trade is regulated under CITES Appendix II.

A biennial or perennial subshrub endemic to the Madeira archipelago. Its very short stem is hidden beneath a flat, plate-like leaf rosette that becomes domed as flowering approaches. It produces pale yellow flowers, occasionally tinged red.

An evergreen climbing shrub endemic to Madeira and the Canary Islands, it is abundant in Madeira's laurel forest. Its leaf-like modified stems bear clusters of small yellow-green flowers along their margins, followed by round red fruits.
A small, hairless or softly hairy subshrub found on Madeira and the Canary Islands. It has small whitish flowers in loose clusters, and its fruit stalks hang downward.

A ground-hugging pea-family plant endemic to Porto Santo in Madeira, Lotus loweanus grows on rocky slopes or hillsides near the ocean. Its narrow leaves have silvery, silky hairs, while its flowers are dark purple and almost black.

Evergreen tree endemic to Madeira and the Canary Islands. Its dark, hard wood smells unpleasant when freshly cut. The fleshy, single-seeded fruit sits partly in a cup-like base, giving it an acorn-like appearance.
Evergreen shrub or small tree endemic to Madeira and the Canary Islands. It has rough white or grey bark, leathery dark-green leaves and olive-like fruit that turns purplish black when ripe.

A semi-evergreen shrub or small tree endemic to Portugal's Madeira and Porto Santo islands, Madeira blueberry grows mainly in crevices, exposed slopes and mountain plains. Its white flowers often have rose stripes, and its berries ripen blue-black and are used in preserves.
edibilityNote: The fruits are used in preserves.

summary: A small tree endemic to Madeira and the Canary Islands, Rhamnus glandulosa is characteristic of laurel forest and often grows near rivers on Madeira. It is uncommon across both island groups and is listed as Vulnerable in the Canaries.
A plant endemic to Macaronesia but now restricted to Madeira following its extinction in the Canary Islands. It is critically endangered because of habitat loss.
A flowering plant endemic to Madeira Island. It grows in scattered, shaded sites in humid valleys, mainly within laurel forests on the island’s northern slope.
A flowering plant endemic to the Madeira Archipelago, Viola paradoxa belongs to the violet family. It is protected under Portuguese or European Community legislation.
A heath native only to Madeira.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and possibly present in the Azores. It grows in scrub, uncultivated ground and rocky places, flowering during June and July.
A herbaceous perennial endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It bears solitary rose-pink, highly fragrant flowers and glossy green leaves with distinctly blue-green undersides.

Perennial flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, occurring in eastern Portugal and central and western Spain. Dense yellow-green glandular hairs make the entire plant very sticky, and its flowers are pink or, rarely, white. All parts are poisonous if ingested.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous when directly ingested.

summary: A large fern native to Macaronesia, with Iberian populations that may have been introduced. Its rhizomes are densely covered in long, silky light-brown hairs, and it favors shady, humid sites near streams or waterfalls.

summary: A perennial grass native to the Azores and Madeira, mainly growing in temperate regions.
Evergreen flowering plant native to South Africa's Eastern Cape Province. It has strap-shaped leaves and hanging clusters of narrow, trumpet-shaped red and yellow flowers tipped with green.

A strong evergreen climbing plant native to southwestern China and Myanmar. In late winter and early spring it produces abundant reddish-pink buds followed by highly fragrant, star-shaped white flowers.

A multi-branched shrub or occasional small tree native to semi-arid highlands around the Red Sea and extending into Kenya and Tanzania, it bears dense clusters of usually bright orange flowers. Its fruits are eaten raw.
edibilityNote: The fruits are eaten raw.

summary: An oak native to parts of southern Europe and the Middle East, it produces hard, corrugated galls on young branches. These galls have long been used medicinally in Asia and for leather softening, black dye and ink; the plant can also thicken stews or be mixed with cereals to make bread.
edibilityNote: The plant can be used to thicken stews or mixed with cereals to make bread.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to the Azores, Portugal. It occurs on all nine islands, growing among coastal rocks and sands and in coastal wasteland.

Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and distributed around the Mediterranean. Within mainland Portugal it has been recorded only in the Algarve, along paths, slopes and abandoned fields; four population groups were recorded over the last quarter-century, but only one was found during Red List fieldwork. It is difficult to identify and may have been overlooked.

summary: A perennial flowering plant endemic to the Azores, occurring on Terceira, São Miguel, São Jorge, Pico, Faial and Flores. It has toothed, conspicuously hairy leaves and one to four yellow flower heads on long stalks.

sources.attribution: Kilian N (2024). Cichorieae Systematics Portal. Botanic Garden and Botanical Museum Berlin. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/gzcrwf accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to the Azores, trifoliate ammi is native to seven of the nine islands. It grows on slopes, in craters and ravines, and in juniper forests.
A herbaceous plant endemic to the Azores, it is protected under the Bern Convention and the European Union's Habitats Directive.
A flowering plant endemic to the Azores. It grows on coastal cliffs and on inland rocks and steep slopes, and is probably extinct on Faial.
A woody-based perennial flowering plant endemic to the Azores, occurring on every island except Graciosa. It has deeply toothed leaves and usually several flower heads on branched stems.
