summary: A perennial native to the Azores and Madeira, with smooth, toothed leaves and yellow flowers scattered along its stems. Older plants develop a woody base.

Rock-growing moss endemic to the Azores. It is dark, glossy green with yellow-green fronds, fine-pointed leaves and an elongated orange-red capsule. It occurs mainly on rocks in sheltered, shady areas of natural forest.

A small perennial herb endemic to the Azores. It has bright green glandular-hairy leaves and white flowers, with scattered coastal populations close to the sea on salt-exposed cliffs. Except on Santa Maria, it is confined to rocky coasts; there it also reaches higher ground and grows in clay and slope deposits.

Perennial plant endemic to Portugal’s Azores, it has deeply cut leaves and dense clusters of small white flowers. It grows on six islands in shady, humid ravines and natural laurel forests, usually above 400 metres.
A sorrel endemic to Portugal’s Azores. Recorded on five islands, it inhabits caldeiras, watercourses and natural meadows, and on São Jorge also occurs in coastal-forest clearings.
A thorny, arching or climbing shrub endemic to the Azores. Its leaves have five strongly domed leaflets, and its large pale pink or white flowers appear in June and July.

sources.title: Rubus hochstetterorum Seub.
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Evergreen shrub or medium-sized tree endemic to the Azores, where it occurs on most islands. It bears small white flowers in clusters from March to July and fleshy, dark blue, olive-like fruits.
A flowering plant endemic to the Azores, it grows on coastal cliffs, in ravines and inside craters. On Santa Maria, it also occurs beside roads and in Pittosporum woods.
A flowering plant found naturally only in the Azores, where it grows on rocks, cliffs and coastal landslides. Most populations occur near sea level, although some on Flores grow higher up.

A flowering plant endemic to the Azores, Portugal, where it occurs on all nine islands. It grows in woods, shrubland, plantations, roadside habitats and bog-moss formations, generally above 200 metres.

A grass-like plant endemic to the Azores, occurring on every island except Santa Maria and Graciosa. It has brown-purple flowers in hanging clusters and usually inhabits moist uplands or native-forest clearings, sometimes growing over moss on tree trunks.
Flowering perennial native to São Miguel Island in the Azores, rigid hawkbit grows to about 40 centimetres and is readily available from commercial suppliers.

A tall perennial herb endemic to the Azores. It forms a basal rosette, produces white flowers and favours moist, sheltered crater slopes, narrow ravines and rock faces. It is classified as endangered.

sources.title: Lactuca watsoniana Trel.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An aquatic fern endemic to the Azores. Its long, narrow leaves form a basal rosette, with solitary spore cases at their bases. It occurs rarely in small, nutrient-poor lakes, generally above 500 metres and often inside craters.

A bushy perennial shrub endemic to the Portuguese Azores, it has many stems and golden-yellow flowers. It often colonizes clearings, landslides and volcanic ash deposits, although local populations usually contain few plants.
A clubmoss, it is a pteridophyte placed in Huperziaceae, though some classifications include it within the broader Lycopodiaceae.
A flowering grass endemic to the Azores, where it occurs on every island except Santa Maria.

An evergreen woody climber endemic to the Azores, Azores ivy uses aerial rootlets to cling to trees, rocks and walls, or spreads as ground cover without supports. Its climbing stems bear lobed juvenile leaves, while sun-exposed flowering stems have unlobed, heart-shaped adult leaves.
A flowering grass endemic to the Azores Archipelago.
Grass endemic to the Azores, Portugal. It grows on coastal cliffs and rocks and occurs on all nine islands.
A flowering plant endemic to the Azores, occurring on every island except Graciosa, Corvo and Santa Maria. It is protected under the Bern Convention and the Habitats Directive.
A sedge native to the Azores, Carex vulcani is generally found above 300 metres.
A plant species endemic to the Azores, Azorean bittercress occurs on every island except Graciosa.
A daisy endemic to the Azores.
A parasitic plant endemic to the Azores, it is restricted to Faial, Pico, São Jorge and Terceira. It grows on the local juniper Juniperus brevifolia.
Flowering plant in the carrot family, endemic to the Azores. It occurs only on São Miguel, Terceira, Pico and Flores.

A stolon-forming perennial grass found in western and southern Iberia and North Africa, especially in wet grasslands and along streams. It has loose, spreading flower heads and flowers from June to July.
A thorny tree native to Africa and the Middle East. Its wood is used for canoes, mortars and pestles, and its seed pods provide livestock feed.
edibilityNote: Food and drink uses are reported, but the supplied source does not specify the parts or preparation.

summary: A flowering plant native to the Canary Islands, it has been introduced to Italy, Sardinia and Sicily.

A vigorous evergreen climber native to the North African coast and its coastal mountains, including those of Algeria, it clings by aerial roots and has reddish stems. Its fertile branches usually have less-lobed leaves than its younger stems. Eating the leaves or berries can cause severe discomfort and mild poisoning.
edibilityNote: The leaves and berries contain hederagenin; ingesting them may cause severe discomfort and mild poisoning.

summary: A plant native to Venezuela, Trinidad and Tobago, and the Netherlands Antilles.
Aloe species native to Ethiopia and Eritrea in Africa. It grows in colonies and bears orange flowers in early spring.
A tree in the ebony family, Diospyros ferrea is found from West Africa across southern and Southeast Asia to Australia, Melanesia and Polynesia, reaching north to Japan’s Ryukyu Islands.
A citrus species native to southern China, it bears the round kumquat fruit.
A flowering vine native to the Philippines. It grows on other plants and has succulent, lance-shaped leaves; variegated forms are sold as houseplants in temperate climates.

A tropical fruit tree native to Mexico, Central America and Colombia, it is an evergreen persimmon. Its tomato-like fruit has inedible skin and unripe white pulp, but when ripe the pulp develops a flavour, colour and texture often compared to chocolate pudding.
edibilityNote: The ripe pulp is edible; the skin and unripe pulp are inedible, and unripe fruit is astringent, caustic, bitter and irritating.

summary: A flowering plant with no explicitly stated native origin, it occurs from Tanzania to South Africa.

A shrubby perennial endemic to Brazil. Its flowers open purple with white throats, fade through lavender to white, and display all three colours together as new blooms appear; the plant is toxic, especially its fruit.
edibilityNote: The plant is toxic, especially its fruit.

summary: An evergreen flowering perennial native to Brazil. Its long, narrow leaves have alternating dark-green and cream bands, with reddish undersides.

An evergreen or semi-evergreen shrub native to subtropical regions and moist forests and meadows of Southeast Asia, from India and China to Japan. Its deep-green leaves smell unpleasant when broken, while pink buds open into abundant white flowers nearly year-round, especially from early spring to autumn.
Fern native mainly to Japan and China. Known as squirrel's-foot fern, it has narrow leaflets and grows well in shady places.

A shrub or dense tree native from Bangladesh and mainland Southeast Asia through Sumatra, Java, Borneo and the Philippines, it is noted for colourful red or pink young leaves. Its flowers are fragrant, and its fruits turn black when fully ripe.

A large evergreen tree native to South and Southeast Asia, Indochina and southern China. Its strongly fragrant cream to yellow-orange flowers bloom from June to September, while its finely textured dark wood is used for furniture, construction and cabinetry.

Low, spreading perennial native to southern Europe and northwest Africa. It may be evergreen or semi-evergreen depending on winter harshness, with snowflake-like white flowers that develop pink or purple tinges as they age.
A flowering plant native to Brazil, monkey plant is an evergreen perennial with hairy, white-veined leaves. It bears trumpet-shaped pink flowers in summer.
An asphodel species endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. One recognized subspecies is endemic to Portugal’s Gardunha range, while another occurs in western central Spain.

A flowering orchid native to Maritime Southeast Asia, New Guinea and Australia, the moth orchid usually grows on trees and rarely on rocks. It has thick, fleshy leaves and branching stems of long-lasting, nearly flat white flowers.
A flowering rush native to Greenland, subarctic and temperate Eurasia, and northwestern Africa.

A large bamboo native to Taiwan and southern China, it has dense foliage, green canes and long leaves. Its crisp, sweet young shoots are highly sought after in Taiwan and China, while the canes are used for furniture but are unsuitable for construction.
edibilityNote: The crisp, sweet young shoots are highly sought after in Taiwan and China.

summary: An evergreen subshrub native to Central America, it has weak stems and large, softly hairy, deeply lobed leaves. Yellow, daisy-like flower heads appear from winter to early spring.

A freshwater green alga with a cosmopolitan distribution. It forms motionless, flat circular colonies with holes between their polygonal cells. Its decay-resistant cell walls have been preserved in lake sediments dating from the Holocene.

A small cormous flowering plant native to eastern and southern Africa, from Kenya to northeastern South Africa, Freesia laxa is also grown as an ornamental. Its fan-shaped leaves surround a flower stalk bearing flattened red, white or pale blue flowers, often with darker markings, followed by bright red seeds.

A tropical flowering water lily native to South America, primarily Brazil, Bolivia, Argentina and Paraguay, Victoria cruziana has very large floating leaves with thick raised rims. Each flower opens white before turning deep pink on its second and final day.

A fan palm native to tropical and subtropical South and Southeast Asia, it is a tall, sturdy tree crowned with large fan-shaped leaves. Its fruit and sprouts are eaten raw or cooked, while its sap is consumed fresh or made into palm wine, sugar, jaggery and candy.
edibilityNote: Fruit and sprouts are eaten raw or cooked; sap is drunk fresh or processed into wine, sugar, jaggery and candy.

summary: A bulb-forming perennial native to the Windward Islands of the eastern Caribbean, green-tinge spiderlily produces clusters of white flowers with a slight green tint. Their narrow petals curl backwards when flowering.
A brush cherry tree native to tropical Asia and Queensland. Its waxy, crisp, bell-shaped fruit is edible and slightly sweet, while the edible leaves are sometimes used to wrap food.
edibilityNote: The cultivated fruit is eaten; the leaves are also edible and sometimes used to wrap food.

summary: Tropical fruit tree native to Melanesia and coastal Southeast Asia. Its oval fruits ripen from hard green to golden yellow and have juicy, crunchy, mildly sour flesh eaten raw or prepared in drinks, preserves, salads and savoury dishes; young or mature leaves are also eaten in some regions.
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten raw or prepared in many dishes and drinks; young or mature leaves are also eaten regionally.

summary: A herbaceous perennial whose native origin is not specified. It has simple leaves on arching stems and branching clusters of pink or white flowers from late summer through autumn in USDA hardiness zone 7.
Fern endemic to the islands of Macaronesia.
Fern native only to the Azores archipelago.
A terrestrial woodland moss; no native origin is supplied. It is long-lived.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A leafy liverwort found globally, MacKay's pouncewort forms colonies of flattened, worm-like shoots across rock surfaces. Its shoots are usually black, with rounded leaves and smaller inflated, toothed lobes.

A flowering plant native to southern and tropical Asia, Madagascar, Malesia and the Pacific Islands, it has pointed leaves and branching underground stems. Its flowers have white petals and orange-yellow anthers, followed by dark blue-purple berries often eaten by native birds.

A perennial flowering subshrub native to a wide area of South America, including Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina. Its mint-green leaves smell of anise when crushed, and its flowers come in shades of blue, sometimes an uncommon true blue.

Deciduous shrub native to Panama, Colombia and Venezuela. It blooms profusely with nearly scentless white flowers with yellow centres and has thick, glossy leaves shaped like a cobra’s hood or spoon. Its leaves are described as toxic.
edibilityNote: The leaves are described as toxic.

summary: A tree native to India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Indochina and southern China, false mangosteen grows in humid forests in valleys and on hills. It has greenish-white flower clusters and yellow fruits with yellow flesh and about five brown seeds.

Flowering palm native to the mountainous forests of India and Bhutan, typically growing on cliffs and hillsides. Its trunk is usually clear of old leaf bases except near the crown, and its feather-like leaves have fewer, less severe spines than other Phoenix species. The yellow-to-orange fruit contains one large seed.

A tropical wetland tree native to eastern Brazil, Pachira glabra grows beside waterways. It has a swollen trunk base and large, fragrant white flowers that open at night and fall by the following afternoon.
edibilityNote: Boiled or roasted seeds are eaten; roasted seeds may make a hot drink. Young leaves and flowers are also eaten.

summary: Orchid native to Northeast India and southern Yunnan in China. Its bluish-purple flowers last notably longer than those of other orchids, and each plant can bear up to 20–30 flower spikes.

A spreading deciduous fern native to southern and western Europe, it grows on shady rocks near Mediterranean coasts and in the mountains of Atlantic Europe. Its divided fronds bear round yellow to orange-yellow spore clusters, which are yellow in winter.

An ornamental bromeliad of unspecified native origin, it is recorded growing in Bahia and Pernambuco, Brazil. Its open upright rosette turns reddish orange after flowering, and the plant blooms only once before dying.
Woody climber endemic to eastern Australia. It has leaves divided into several egg-shaped leaflets and white or pink trumpet-shaped flowers that are red and hairy inside.

Herbaceous perennial native to the eastern Mediterranean, southwestern Asia, southeastern Europe and northeastern Africa. Its hairy leaves become more deeply divided higher on the stems, which bear red, pink, yellow or white flowers.

A perennial bulb found across the Mediterranean, Bellevalia dubia has low-lying leaves. Its cylindrical, bell-shaped flowers change from sky blue to grey-violet or brownish, with white tips marked by green veins. It flowers from March to April.

Clumping bamboo native to southern Asia, including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Indochina. It forms dense, heavily branched thickets with bright green, curved, spiny canes and deep-purple young shoots.

A flowering plant of unspecified native origin. It usually blooms from August to October with yellow or white flowers and yellow pollen. Its flower heads, flowers, young leaves and petals are eaten after preparations including pickling, brewing, cooking or blanching.
edibilityNote: Flower heads are pickled in vinegar; flowers make tea, young leaves are steeped or cooked, and petals are blanched for dishes.

summary: An aromatic shrub endemic to Cape Verde. It bears small yellow flowers and grows on plains and stony slopes across Santo Antão, Santiago and Fogo, from semi-arid to humid zones.
A Kalanchoe species, this plant has completely green leaves, unlike K. daigremontiana, which has bands or spots on the leaf backs.

A delicate scrambling plant endemic to Europe, mainly near the Atlantic fringe. Usually annual but occasionally perennial, it climbs with branching leaf tendrils and bears small creamy-yellow flowers.
A flowering plant endemic to Madeira. It is introduced in mainland Portugal and is protected under Portuguese or European legislation.

sources.title: Sibthorpia peregrina L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Flowering, aromatic shrub with no native origin specified. It is a softly hairy, partly woody weed of disturbed ground and grasslands, with toothed leaves and loose yellow flower heads. In several Asian traditions it is used medicinally, including for cold symptoms, wounds and stomach pain.
edibilityNote: A citation-needed account says the Bodos of Assam add it to soups, chicken and curries, or serve it with chillies and soda-ash water.

summary: A vine endemic to the Philippines, found beside streams in damp forests and ravines. It bears cascading clusters of vivid turquoise or greenish-blue, claw-shaped flowers. The flowers are edible and are eaten as vegetables on Luzon.
edibilityNote: People on Luzon eat the flowers as vegetables, similarly to katurai.

summary: A shrub occurring across southern Europe and North Africa as far as Mauritania. In mainland Portugal it grows in coastal scrub and directly on sea cliffs, with the known plants concentrated in one declining population.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, where its distribution is restricted to the Algarve Barrocal. It grows in dry clearings among open scrub on rocky, limestone soils.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A cactus native to southern Brazil. Its heavily ribbed, spiny stems range from spherical to column-like and bear pale yellow summer flowers; its sparse, fragmented populations are classified as Endangered.

A plant endemic to Iberia, it occurs locally in Portugal from Baixo Alentejo to Trás-os-Montes, growing in rock cracks along watercourses and flood channels. In the 2016–2019 mainland Portugal assessment, its seven small subpopulations were classed as Vulnerable amid continuing declines and habitat loss.

summary: An evergreen flowering shrub endemic to rocky sandstone slopes in South Africa’s Western Cape, it has silvery-green hairy leaves and yellow daisy-like flowers. Flowering lasts from early summer into autumn, and may continue into winter in mild climates.

A perennial rosette plant or small shrub found throughout the Mediterranean; its native origin is not stated. Its narrow, spoon-shaped leaves accompany branched flower clusters from June to October. It grows in coastal sand, rock and dune hollows, as well as steppe grassland.

summary: Tuberous flowering plant native to Mediterranean countries of southern Europe, Western Asia and North Africa, as well as Terceira in the Azores and Ireland.

Carnivorous plant native across continental Southeast Asia, the Malay Archipelago and northern Australia. It has the widest range of any Nepenthes and highly variable pitchers; the Borneo-endemic variety echinostoma has an exceptionally wide pitcher rim.
A flowering grass whose subspecies Festuca brigantina subsp. brigantina is endemic to mainland Portugal. This subspecies is protected under Annexes II and IV of the Habitats Directive.

A tall bamboo native to the Indian subcontinent, Indochina, Tibet and Yunnan. Its dull-green canes mature grey-green and have very thick walls and exceptional tensile strength. It is used extensively by India’s paper-pulp industry.

A flowering perennial bulbous plant native to northeastern, southern and southeastern Brazil, the striped Barbados lily generally bears two to four relatively small, bright red flowers, each with a green stripe extending halfway along its segments. It also produces numerous small bulbs that help it escape cultivation and become established in tropical areas.
A flowering shrub native only to China’s Guizhou and Sichuan provinces. It has golden-yellow flowers without a red tint and thick, paper-like leaves marked with streaks and dots.

An evergreen shrub found along the coasts of Spain, Italy, Croatia and Albania, silverbush forms a low mound rather than a vine. Fine hairs give its grey-green leaves a silvery look, while pink buds open into white, yellow-throated flowers from spring into summer.
A low, spreading shrub endemic to southern Australia, including Flinders Island. Its long trailing stems can form mats, bearing fleshy leaves and white star-shaped flowers marked with purple spots.

A woody evergreen climber native to China, India, Japan, Korea, Indochina and Malaysia, it grows naturally in mountain forests and scrub, often attached to trees. It has glossy leaves and strongly scented cream flowers with a yellow centre; cut stems release milky white latex.

A compact perennial shrub native to Japan. Coarse, dark-green leaves densely cover its rough stems. White to pale-pink flowers appear in spring and sometimes summer, followed by red autumn berries that attract wildlife.

A compact evergreen succulent native to South Africa’s Western Cape, this endangered aloe is confined in the wild to dry clay soils in threatened vegetation. It forms clumps of grey-blue rosettes with short, thick leaves edged by soft white teeth, and produces bright red flowers in November.

A hairless, many-stemmed succulent endemic to South Africa’s Western and Eastern Cape. Its ribbed, cactus-like stems are usually club-shaped and branch near the base. The ‘Snowflake’ cultivar has an exceptionally heavy natural wax coating that gives its stems a whitened appearance.
A succulent plant whose native origin is not stated in the supplied information. Its flowers are visited by the bee Fidelia kobrowi.

A small to medium-sized tree native to Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland, Australia, kurrajong grows from wet coastal districts to semi-arid interiors. It has water-storing trunks, variable-shaped leaves and bell-shaped cream-to-pink flowers; Aboriginal peoples also roasted its seeds after removing the irritating hairs.
edibilityNote: Aboriginal peoples removed irritating hairs from the pods, cleaned and roasted the seeds; European settlers roasted and crushed seeds as a coffee supplement.

summary: A flowering tree of unspecified native origin, it has been recorded across parts of South, Southeast and East Asia. It is commonly grown as an ornamental in Australia, where it is invasive.

A tufted flowering perennial endemic to Mpumalanga, Limpopo and Eswatini in southeastern Africa, the Barberton daisy grows on rocky woodland slopes, usually with some shade. Its deeply wavy or lobed leaves form a rosette, and its showy flowers are normally orange-red but are rarely yellow, orange, white or pink.
A flowering plant native to Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands, it has been bred and hybridised as a garden plant. Cultivated forms are sold in a wide variety of flower and leaf colours.

A mat-forming perennial herb found across parts of southern Australia, including Tasmania. It has mostly egg-shaped leaves and fan-shaped blue, mauve or white flowers with yellow centres, appearing mainly from August to October.

An evergreen shrub or small tree native to Japan and Korea, it has opposite oval leaves with finely toothed tips. Its inconspicuous greenish-white flowers are followed by brown to reddish-brown capsules containing seeds with orange-red coverings.

A low evergreen shrub native to New Zealand and the Australian states of Tasmania, New South Wales and Victoria, creeping wire vine forms wiry mats. It has thin red-brown stems, small glossy leaves and inconspicuous yellowish-white flowers, followed by shiny black fruit in late summer to autumn.
A spreading plant native across coastal Australia. Its succulent, flattened leaves range from light green to purplish red, and it grows along shorelines, estuaries and salt marshes.

A terrestrial fern found in eastern Australia and Norfolk Island, it grows in rainforest, eucalyptus forest and other open forests. Its rough, toothed fronds emerge pinkish to reddish before turning green and may form dense colonies.

Shrub with no explicitly stated native origin, recorded near the coast in eastern Australia. Its white, hairy flowers have split upper petals and orange-to-purple spots below. It is notably tough and grows on cliffs beside the ocean.

Flowering shrub or small tree endemic to eastern Australia. It has finely pointed leaves and sweet-scented white flowers with rows of purple spots, followed by rough, wrinkled dark blue or purple fruit.
Highly aromatic shrub endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula. Branched hairs make its leaves and flowering parts sticky, while its small white flowers quickly turn brown.

A small evergreen shrub native to Europe, northern Africa and western Asia, it grows in salty coastal habitats. Its silvery grey leaves have white deposits, while its summer flowers range from pink and lavender to purple before fading violet.
A plant endemic to Brazil. It bears clusters of pink flowers.
A plant species endemic to Chile. Its varieties differ in whether the floral bracts extend beyond the sepals or flower stalks and whether the flower cluster remains densely white-hairy.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Aquatic plant found wild across tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. Its narrow leaves range from pale green to reddish, while runners can form dense stands. It can be eaten when steamed or boiled.
edibilityNote: The plant can be eaten after steaming or boiling; no specific edible part is identified.

summary: A moss reported from Australasia and the Pacific. Recorded settings include gardens, greenhouses, inland cliffs, rock pavements, outcrops and sublittoral sediment.

summary: A moss endemic to the mountains of Europe, icy rock-moss grows in humid, rocky alpine and subalpine habitats. In Britain it typically occurs on rocks in streams fed by snow patches.

A deciduous tree native to the eastern Mediterranean, Oriental sweetgum occurs mainly in floodplain stands in southwestern Turkey and on Rhodes. Its colourful autumn leaves are especially valued, and sap obtained from June to September is softened, pressed and made into an aromatic balsam or distilled oil.

An amphibious annual plant native to the Mediterranean Basin. It produces grass-like submerged leaves, spoon-shaped floating leaves or lance-shaped emergent leaves depending on water depth, and in Portugal it is now restricted to two areas.

summary: A deciduous tree originating around the Yangtze River in southern China. Its strongly fragrant white, pink or red flowers open in mid-winter, before the leaves. Across East Asian cuisines, the fruit is used in juices, sauces and alcohol, or prepared by pickling or drying.
edibilityNote: The fruit is used in East Asian juices, sauces and alcoholic drinks, and may be pickled or dried.

summary: A flowering plant whose range extends from eastern South Africa and Madagascar through tropical Africa to western Arabia. It produces tall spikes of yellow to scarlet flowers, often red-streaked over yellow, and is the principal parent of large-flowered grandiflora hybrids.

Shrub or small tree native to China, Korea, Taiwan, Japan, the Himalayan region of India, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines. It bears fragrant white flower clusters in spring, followed by red berries that mature to black.

A shrub occurring widely from eastern and southeastern Asia through New Guinea to northern Australia and the Solomon Islands, it sheds its leaves during the dry season. Its slender, straggling branches bear small white flowers and fruits that ripen brownish orange.

A perennial subshrub native to the western and central Mediterranean, it occurs mainly on cliffs and rocky coasts. Its stiff, branched stems and deeply lobed leaves are coated in grey-white woolly hairs, while its flowers are yellow and daisy-like.

An annual herb native to western Asia and southern Europe, yellow pheasant's-eye has finely divided foliage and red flowers with black centres. In mainland Portugal it grows among traditional dryland crops and was assessed as Vulnerable because of its limited range, few locations and continuing decline.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: An Arctic–alpine rosette-forming plant distributed from eastern Canada to Russia and in southern European mountains, it grows in damp places such as stream edges and wet rock ledges. Its loose flower clusters have white petals marked near the base with yellow or red spots.
An Asian fig tree native from Assam to Taiwan, through Southeast Asia, Malesia and New Guinea. Male and female flowers grow on separate trees, and its fruit becomes greenish yellow when ripe.

A flowering plant native to northeastern Spain, southern France and Italy, Crimean iris grows on rocky or sandy hillsides and in woodland. It produces yellow or violet flowers in March and April and prefers dry conditions during its summer dormancy.

An orchid native to Mediterranean southern Europe and northern Africa, with its range extending east to Iran and Turkmenistan. Its three recognized subspecies occupy distinct western Mediterranean, central and eastern Mediterranean, and Turkey-to-Central Asian ranges.
A flowering plant with no stated native origin, goat pea belongs to the pea family and is introduced in mainland Portugal.
A perennial bulb native to Spain and France and naturalised in Turkey. It is low-growing, with yellow flowers that have a slightly lemony fragrance.
Fast-growing deciduous climbing plant native to East Asia. It bears large orange trumpet-shaped flowers in summer and attaches to porous surfaces using scattered aerial roots.

An annual flowering herb native to the desert southwest of North America and northern and central Mexico. Its foliage is hairy, and its bright purple, lavender or pink bell-shaped flowers grow alone or in small clusters.
A fast-growing tree native to Africa. It has dark grey to grey-brown bark, reddish-brown heartwood, spirally arranged leaves clustered at branch ends, and sweet-scented white flowers.

Annual herb native to Africa, southern Europe, and parts of Asia from East Asia to India and Central Asia. Its leaves, stems and seeds can be eaten raw or cooked, though leaves may concentrate nitrates when grown on nitrogen-rich soil.
edibilityNote: Leaves, stems and seeds are eaten raw or cooked; leaves are widely used as a vegetable, often in sauces and stews.

summary: An ornamental tree native to parts of Asia, including Korea, Taiwan, mid-southern China and Japan’s Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, Ilex integra has light-yellow flowers. Its bark is used in birdlime, and it is sometimes planted as a sacred tree.

A perennial flowering plant native to Europe and parts of North Africa, parsley water-dropwort inhabits mainly coastal wetlands and some inland freshwater marshes. Its lower leaves are parsley-like, its leaf stalks smell of celery, and it bears white flowers from June to September in northern Europe. No part is edible by humans.
edibilityNote: No part of the plant is edible by humans.

summary: A perennial flowering plant found across western, central and southeastern Europe, including the British Isles. It grows mainly in damp, neutral grasslands and has stout woody roots and small yellowish flowers.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. There it grows in heath and other acid-loving scrub or beneath deciduous woodland, usually on siliceous ground.

sources.title: Physospermum cornubiense (L.) DC.
sources.attribution: Jeanmonod D, Schlüssel A, carolina (2012). Notes et contributions à la flore de Corse, XXIV. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15553/c2012v672a11 accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual plant distributed from central Europe to western Asia, mostly near coasts. It is delicate and often much-branched, with blue-green narrow leaves and tiny yellowish to orange flowers, and favors damp or disturbed salty ground.

sources.title: Bupleurum tenuissimum L.
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A herbaceous perennial native to the UK and found mainly in Central and Southern Europe, hog's fennel is rare in Britain and now limited to parts of Essex and Kent. Its greenish-yellow flower clusters rise above dark green leaves, while its stout root releases strongly sulphur-scented latex when cut in spring.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It belongs to the family Apiaceae and is not protected under Portuguese or European Community legislation.

An annual or biennial flowering plant native to southern and south-central Europe, though probably not native in northern parts of its range. It is hairy or bristly, with a hollow ridged stem and flat clusters of white flowers whose outer petals are conspicuously longer.
A fern found locally along Europe's Atlantic seaboard. It was first recorded in Britain in February 2000 beside Cornwall's River Camel.
A perennial fern confined to Atlantic coastal western Europe and Macaronesia. Its pale yellow-green, often arching fronds have a characteristically crisped appearance and a hay-like scent.

A robust deciduous or partly evergreen fern native mainly to western and central Europe, broad buckler-fern occurs chiefly in mountains in southern Europe and also between the Black and Caspian seas. Its dark green, finely divided fronds have ribs covered with brown scales.

A perennial flowering plant occurring across western Europe. It has spear-shaped, widely toothed leaves and white flowers that fade to pink, blooming from June to August; it is easily confused with two other willowherbs.
A flowering plant native from Europe to China. It is common in moist, disturbed lowland sites and can be difficult to distinguish from several other willowherbs.

A wild rose native to Western, Central and Southern Europe, the field rose is a vigorous, thorny, rambling shrub with long, arching or scrambling purple stems. It bears slightly fragrant, creamy-white flowers in a single midsummer flush, followed by oval orange-red hips.

Perennial mint-family herb native to Western Europe and North Africa. The nominate subspecies is tufted, hairy and mint-scented, with dark green leaves and relatively large, dark flowers. The leaves can be infused for aromatic tea or added to cooked foods for a pungent flavour likened to marjoram and mint.
edibilityNote: Leaves can be infused as aromatic tea or added to cooked food for a pungent, marjoram-and-mint-like flavour.

summary: A dense, upright flowering shrub endemic to near-coastal southwestern Western Australia. It has narrow elliptical leaves and head-like clusters of pale to deep pink tubular flowers, blooming mainly from August to February. It grows on coastal dunes and rocky headlands.
A plant of unspecified native origin, found in Sicily, Greece and Turkey. It has a flavor similar to common oregano and is reported to have antimicrobial activity.

A perennial plant of unspecified native origin, bush basil is valued in Portugal for its pleasant smell. Known there as manjerico, it is traditionally sold in small decorated pots during June’s Santos Populares celebrations and was given by men to their lovers.
A short-stemmed South African plant, Goat's-foot has bluish flowers.
A perennial plant with underground storage organs, endemic to South Africa’s Eastern and Western Cape and associated with fynbos. It bears red-purple flowers from April to July.

sources.title: Chasmanthe aethiopica (L.) N.E.Br.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A perennial flowering plant whose native origin is not stated, falling stars is widely distributed across southern and eastern Africa from South Africa to Sudan. It forms large colonies in moist, shady forests and along riverbanks, producing bright orange-to-red flowers from June through August.
A flowering plant native to the temperate and subtropical Northern Hemisphere and Southern Africa, carpet cinquefoil belongs to the rose family.
A red seaweed found in European waters.

A herbaceous perennial native to Mexico, the Caribbean, West Africa, Central America and much of South America. It has broad, fleshy leaves and small pink flowers, and is widely grown in tropical regions as a leaf vegetable. In India’s Mithila region, the leaves are prepared as vegetables and fritters.
edibilityNote: The leaves are widely grown as a vegetable and are prepared as vegetables and fritters in the Mithila region.

summary: A flowering plant native to East and Southeast Asia, Asian taro has large, light-green, diamond- to teardrop-shaped leaves. Its flowers produce a sweet scent that is strongest at night.
edibilityNote: Leaves and stems are eaten cooked as vegetables; the corm is sometimes boiled and mashed. No part should be eaten raw or undercooked.

summary: A deciduous flowering shrub native to dense forests from the Himalayas through southern China to Taiwan. It has coarse, broadly oval leaves and large, flat flower heads in late summer, typically pale blue or pink with white or pale pink florets around the edges.

An evergreen coastal tree native to southern and eastern Africa, white milkwood has dense foliage and small, foul-smelling greenish flowers. Its purplish-black berries are edible, and both the berries and leathery leaves contain milky latex.
edibilityNote: The purplish-black berries are edible.

summary: Upright perennial herb native to the Mediterranean, including Algeria, Morocco, Portugal, Spain and Sicily. It has a woody base, oval leaves and dense cushions of violet-purple summer flowers; cultivated forms also flower in white, red, pink or dark purple.

A herbaceous perennial in the bedstraw and coffee family. Tiny hooks on its leaves and stems let it climb. Its long roots, harvested after two years, have supplied red textile dyes since ancient times.
edibilityNote: Root-derived dyes have been used as food ingredients.

summary: A fern species in the family Pteridaceae.

Grass thought to have originated in China, although genomic evidence suggests separate domestication of naked and hulled oats in China and Europe. Its edible seeds readily shed their hulls when threshed.
edibilityNote: Seeds are edible; naked oats have long been used as food, while Cornish grain was sprouted, dried and crushed for porridge, puddings and ale.

summary: Fast-growing shrub or small tree endemic to eastern Australia. It has pale green, narrowly oval leaves and white to pale-yellow flower clusters; its egg-shaped fruits are covered with black, blister-like warts.
Flowering plant native to southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa, including the Iberian Peninsula, Balearic Islands, parts of North Africa, Sardinia, and northern and central Italy.

A flowering plant found around much of the central Mediterranean Basin, Mediterranean meadow saffron produces abundant small pink-to-purple flowers and foliage in autumn. Its variable flowers may open flat like stars or remain cup-shaped.
A subshrub native to Portugal, Spain and France. It usually has several stems and pale lilac to whitish petals that are fringed only halfway.

sources.title: Dianthus hyssopifolius L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A poisonous nightshade native to several African countries, including Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa, Zimbabwe and Mozambique, it has tomato-like fruits that are green when raw and yellow when ripe. In eastern Kenya, village children cautiously use the poisonous yellow fruits as footballs.
edibilityNote: The plant and its yellow fruits are described as poisonous; no qualified human food use is given.

summary: A fast-growing, branching cactus found in Bolivia, Paraguay, southern Brazil, northern Argentina and Uruguay. It may bear straight white spines, orange-to-yellow flowers from late spring into summer, and club-shaped fruit that ripens purple-red.
Succulent flowering plant native to South Africa. It forms a dense scrambling or climbing growth with glossy, fleshy, coarsely toothed leaves and clusters of honey-scented yellow flowers.

Perennial climber native to southern Africa, from South Africa’s coastal Eastern Cape to eastern Zimbabwe. It has bright green, fleshy, ivy-like leaves with purple veins and produces cinnamon-scented, bright yellow, daisy-like flowers, generally from mid-autumn to winter.

A perennial grass native to most of Europe, southwestern Asia and northwestern Africa. It has densely packed flowerheads and is much smaller than Timothy grass, with which it is often confused; it flowers from June to August.

A perennial fern native across much of Asia, Australia, New Zealand and Polynesia. Gray hairs mark the undersides of its leaves, while long rhizomes help it form thick ground cover; outside its native range it is invasive in several regions.
A very large palm native to peninsular Thailand, it has exceptionally long, twice-divided fronds bearing thousands of fan- or wedge-shaped leaflets.

A palm native to southern Brazil, Uruguay and northern Argentina. Its solitary trunk often leans and commonly retains old leaf bases for years. The ripe fruit may be yellow, orange, red or purple, with sweet, juicy, slightly fibrous flesh that is edible.
edibilityNote: The sweet fruit is edible; ripe flesh is described as juicy and slightly fibrous.

summary: Slow-growing palm native to southernmost Brazil and Uruguay. Its feather-like leaves arch toward a thick, stout trunk. The highly aromatic fruit varies in colour and sweet-sour flavour, and the larger-fruited pulposa type is commonly cultivated locally for food.
edibilityNote: The aromatic ripe fruit is eaten; larger-fruited pulposa-type palms are cultivated in Brazilian and Uruguayan orchards.

summary: A small palm endemic to the highlands of southern Brazil. Its flower-bearing woody sheath is densely covered with distinctive rust-coloured woolly hairs, and its leaves arch back toward the trunk. Locally, the fruit pulp is used to make beverages, wine, juice, jellies and jams.
edibilityNote: Fruit pulp is used locally to make beverages, wine, juice, jellies and jams.

summary: A palm native to the Mascarene Islands. It has a solitary ringed trunk and a swollen, white-waxy crown base, while its oval fruits ripen purple or black.
A tall, slender palm native to Central and South America and Trinidad and Tobago. It produces edible açaí fruit and hearts of palm, although taking the heart kills this usually single-stemmed tree.
edibilityNote: The fruit is edible and used for beverages; the heart of palm is also eaten, but harvesting it kills the single-stemmed tree.

summary: Palm endemic to Lord Howe Island, Australia. Mature crowns contain roughly 36 leaves, and the species is restricted to the island's volcanic soils.

A fan palm native to parts of South and Southeast Asia and Yunnan, China. It has large fan-shaped leaves with downward-curving spines on their stalks, and leaden-blue fruits that are broader than long.

A flowering palm indigenous to southern Asia, Phoenix loureiroi grows in forests and open terrain from sea level to high elevations. Its sharply pointed leaflets form stiff, feathery leaves, while its ripe fruit is bluish-black and usually hidden within the leaf crown.

A palm native to the eastern Mediterranean, particularly the southernmost parts of Greece and Turkey, Phoenix theophrasti usually has several slender stems. Its thin, fibrous, acrid fruits are usually inedible, although local people sometimes eat them.
edibilityNote: The usually inedible fruits have thin, fibrous, acrid pulp but are sometimes eaten by local people.

summary: A palm native to southern Pakistan, most of India, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar and Bangladesh, it bears single-seeded fruit that ripens purple-red. The fruit is made into wine and jelly, while tapped sap is drunk fresh or fermented into toddy and, in West Bengal and Bangladesh, boiled into palm jaggery.
edibilityNote: Fruit is made into wine and jelly; sap is drunk fresh, fermented into toddy or boiled into jaggery in West Bengal and Bangladesh.

summary: A palm native to Norfolk Island and New Zealand’s Kermadec Islands, it has long feather-like leaves and bright red ripe fruit. Early Norfolk Island settlers used its growing tip as a vegetable, raw or boiled.
edibilityNote: Early Norfolk Island settlers ate the growing tip as a vegetable, either raw or boiled.

summary: A palm tree known from two distinct populations in the Khasia Hills of northeast India and central northern Nepal, with others reported in Assam, Sikkim, Burma and southern China. Its leaves split regularly about halfway, and its coffee-bean-shaped seeds grow above a bare rather than fibrous trunk.

A corm-forming flowering perennial native to eastern Africa from Ethiopia to Mozambique. In late summer it bears numerous fragrant white flowers with maroon, or occasionally orange, throat markings on slender nodding stems.

A flowering plant endemic to South Africa and southern Namibia, Stapelia hirsuta has grooved, roughly four-angled stems. Its flat, very hairy dark-red flowers resemble rotting meat and produce a carrion smell that attracts flies.

A rhizomatous flowering perennial native to Brazil’s tropical forests. Its striking oval leaves lie flat by day and fold upright at night, while its spreading stems root at leaf nodes and carpet the forest floor.

An evergreen broadleaf tree endemic to New Zealand. Its inconspicuous flowers are followed by dark-purple fruit; Māori traditionally ate both the flesh and kernels after lengthy steaming, washing and further preparation.
edibilityNote: Māori traditionally ate the flesh and kernels; berries were steamed for two days, washed, and the dried kernels later soaked and pounded.

summary: A climbing plant endemic to New Zealand, Parsonsia heterophylla has leaves whose shapes vary greatly, especially in young plants. Its usually white, scented tubular flowers grow in compact clusters and may be noticed more readily by smell than sight.

An epiphytic orchid endemic to Madagascar, it bears star-shaped, waxy flowers with remarkably long nectar spurs. The flowers release an intense spicy scent only at night and change from green to white before yellowing as they wilt.

Single-celled alga found in tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide. One of the largest known unicellular organisms, it forms a smooth, glassy bubble that can appear green, silver, teal or nearly black.

A compact evergreen shrub native to southern Argentina and Chile. It has glossy leaves, solitary white spring flowers, and showy autumn berries ranging from deep purple through pink to white; male and female plants must grow together for fruit. The ripe fruit is edible, sweet, juicy, and somewhat tasteless.
edibilityNote: The ripe fruit is edible, sweet, and juicy but somewhat tasteless, and is described as useful survival food.

summary: A flowering grass whose variety duriotagana is endemic to mainland Portugal and variety barbata is native there. Both varieties are protected under Portuguese or European legislation.

Evergreen perennial shrub endemic to central coastal Portugal. It grows on coastal dunes and cliffs, with many branches covered in dry leaves and flowers ranging from pink or white to sometimes purple. Flowering occurs from February to May.

A perennial plant from central and south-central Madagascar, it grows in rocky, sunny places and is the only runner-forming member of its genus. Its few, very thick fleshy leaves form terminal rosettes, and its flowers range from white through pink to purple.

A flowering plant with underground stems, native to Algeria, Greece, Turkey, western Syria and Tunisia. Its evergreen, grass-like leaves accompany fragrant pale lilac or purple flowers marked with a central yellow band. The flowers appear in winter and early spring.
Semievergreen flowering perennial native to Southern Africa and Zimbabwe. It has slender, lance-shaped leaves and spikes of red flowers, occasionally pink or white, from late summer to autumn.

A tropical herbaceous plant native to eastern Africa, from southern Kenya to northeastern South Africa. It has a succulent tuber and glossy dark-green leaves, and may shed its normally evergreen foliage during drought. All parts are poisonous if eaten.
edibilityNote: All parts of the plant are poisonous if ingested.

summary: A deciduous broad-leaved tree whose native origin is not stated, it is common along Himalayan lowlands from Kashmir to western Nepal. It has abundant white flowers and forms a rounded canopy. Its seeds are dried and ground into bitter flour, with the saponins thoroughly washed out before cooking.
edibilityNote: Seeds are dried and ground; bitter saponins are thoroughly washed out before the flour is used in chapatis, halwa or porridge.

summary: A bulbous perennial native to South Africa’s eastern Cape. It has narrow, grasslike, nearly evergreen leaves and autumn clusters of slender pink flowers with crinkled petals.
A corm-forming flowering plant endemic to South Africa’s Western Cape. It grows beside waterfalls in the region’s south-western mountains.

A bulbous flowering plant native to South Africa, pregnant onion may also be native or introduced in tropical East Africa. Its largely exposed bulb produces small bulblets, while tall flower stalks carry many fragrant, green-striped white flowers; most parts are considered toxic to humans.
Flowering plant; the subspecies lowei is native only to Madeira.

A perennial succulent native to Tanzania in eastern Africa, the red dragon flower forms clumps of smooth, square green-to-reddish stems with soft tooth-like bumps. Its small, velvety crimson or burgundy flowers are funnel-shaped and notably lack the rotting-meat smell associated with many other Huernia species.

An evergreen shrub native to Korea, Japan and Taiwan. It has glossy oval leaves and scented white flowers, sometimes tinged pink, in early summer; unlike most Rhaphiolepis species, its fruits are inedible.
edibilityNote: Its fruits are explicitly described as inedible.

summary: A large hazel tree native to the Balkan Peninsula and western Asia, with thick, corky bark. Its small nuts have very hard shells and grow in clusters surrounded by bristly husks.
edibilityNote: The nuts are edible and sometimes gathered, but are small and enclosed in very hard, thick shells.

summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree native to Malesia, Papuasia, the Northern Territory and Queensland. Its young twigs, leaves and flowers have dense rusty-brown hairs, while its yellow or orange capsules contain red seeds held in a sticky ball.
Aquatic fern found mostly in Australia and nearby New Caledonia. It has broad, clover-like fronds and floats in deeper freshwater than other ferns in its genus.

A small fig tree native to eastern Australia, where it grows mainly along waterways and gullies. Its leaves feel like sandpaper, while its succulent oval fruit is densely hairy and was eaten by local Aboriginal people.
edibilityNote: The palatable fruit was eaten by local Aboriginal people.

summary: A spreading woodland tree native to Africa south of the Zambezi River, the weeping boer-bean occurs mainly at middle altitudes. Its bright-red new leaves fade through bronze to dark green, followed by deep-red flowers that may release enough nectar to drip when shaken.

Medium-sized fruit-bearing tree native to Malesia, Australia and the Pacific Islands. Its ripe fruit is edible but tart and may be eaten raw, cooked or preserved; Indigenous Australians buried it underground to ripen.
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is tart and eaten raw, cooked or preserved; Indigenous Australians buried it underground to ripen.

summary: Perennial grass native to parts of Africa, Arabia and Sri Lanka. It grows in stiff, upright tufts with olive-green leaves and densely packed grey-brown flower heads. Its many seeds become sticky when wet and can attach to animals, clothing and machinery.

Small fern widespread across Australia and South Pacific islands. It grows beside streams and along rainforest margins or in other moist forests, with round spore clusters under hairy closed coverings. In Hawaii, it was first recorded as naturalised on Oahu in 1887 and now occurs on all major islands.
edibilityNote: Described as an edible fern; no part or preparation is specified.

summary: A rainforest and woodland tree native to Queensland and New South Wales, Australia, it produces fragrant flower clusters in spring. The cream flowers turn yellow with age and are followed by long, pear-shaped seed capsules.

A flowering plant native to the Arabian Peninsula and much of tropical and subtropical Asia, bearded knotweed is usually described as an erect or sometimes prostrate annual herb with hairless, grooved stems and lance-shaped leaves. Some descriptions instead call it a perennial growing from a creeping rootstock.

A trailing flowering plant native to Australia and Asia. Its stems begin horizontally before turning upright, and it dies back in winter but regenerates after rain. In Africa it is eaten locally during famines.
edibilityNote: Eaten locally in Africa during times of famine.

summary: A tropical tree whose precise native origin is unclear because people spread it early. It bears fruit containing a soft, white, oily kernel inside a hard shell. The nut is mildly toxic raw but is eaten cooked or toasted in many cultures, including in Southeast Asian curries and Hawaiian ʻinamona.
edibilityNote: The nut is mildly toxic raw; cooking or toasting reduces toxicity, after which it is used in Southeast Asian and Hawaiian foods.

summary: An annual or biennial plant native from South America to Mexico, tall fleabane has rather hairy stems and many small flower heads in loose, branching clusters that widen toward the top. Its ray petals are inconspicuous and sometimes tinged purple.

A small fern endemic to Australia, Adiantum atroviride occurs in the Northern Territory, Queensland and New South Wales. Its loosely clustered fronds have shiny black stalks and fan-shaped divisions with shallow lobes.

A perennial tropical grass native to African grasslands, Napier grass forms tall, robust, bamboo-like clumps. Its seeds rarely develop fully, so it usually spreads through horizontal shoots, and its young leaves and shoots are cooked in soups and stews.
edibilityNote: Young leaves and shoots are edible when cooked in soups and stews.

summary: A flowering plant with no explicitly stated native origin, it occurs in Spain, the Canary Islands, Algeria, Morocco, Mauritania and Cape Verde.
A plant species native to southern Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina.

An evergreen shrub or small tree native to Assam, Cambodia, China, the Himalayas, Hainan, Japan, Myanmar, Taiwan, Nepal, Thailand and Vietnam, sweet olive bears strongly fragrant white, yellow or orange-yellow flowers in late summer and autumn. In Chinese cuisine, the flowers may be infused with tea and are also used in jams, cakes, dumplings, soups, liquor and traditional desserts.
edibilityNote: In Chinese cuisine, the flowers may be infused with tea and are used in jams, cakes, dumplings, soups, liquor and traditional desserts.

summary: A strongly aromatic shrub native to the western Mediterranean basin, it has a more pungent, camphor-rich scent than English lavender. Pale lilac flower spikes appear from June to September, depending on the weather.

A perennial herb native to Europe and western Asia, water dock grows beside fresh or coastal waters. It is the tallest dock species, with tough flowering stems that redden with age and large, tapering leaves.
A flowering plant native to Atlantic Europe, St. Dabeoc's heath is abundant in western Ireland and has become naturalised in parts of Great Britain and the Iberian Peninsula.
A tree native to the Caucasian region. It forms a rounded crown of widely spreading branches and bears long, feather-like leaves and green winged nuts in hanging clusters.

Shrub or small tree endemic to the upper Amazon region at the eastern base of the Andes in Peru. It has large, fragrant, nodding, funnel-shaped flowers in shades of white and pink, with a very narrow, unusually long tube at the base.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous.

summary: An evergreen shrub native to the Atlantic coasts of western Europe. Its green, spiny stems largely take over the work of its reduced leaves, and yellow flowers appear mainly in late summer and autumn. It can regrow from its roots after fire, while slight scorching encourages seed germination.

An upright annual clover native to mainland Portugal. It has glossy, toothed leaflets and pink flowers in small rounded heads, and grows in temporarily waterlogged pastures and meadows on siliceous ground.

sources.title: Trifolium strictum L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual clover native to mainland Portugal and introduced to Madeira. It grows in annual grasslands, generally on poor, dry, siliceous soils.

An annual flowering herb native across parts of Europe, western and Central Asia, and northern and eastern Africa, this sandwort has a low, spreading habit. It produces white flowers from late winter to spring.

Slender annual herb native to Eurasia and introduced into North America. Its leaves usually have three conspicuous lengthwise veins, sometimes as many as five, and its sepals are longer than its petals.
Flowering plant in the carnation family; only its robusta subspecies is explicitly described here as native to mainland Portugal.

A rhizomatous perennial grass native to southern Europe and North Africa. Its stiff, threadlike leaves are distinctive, and its strong, flexible fibres are used for ropes, sandals, baskets, mats and paper.
A short-lived coastal herb, sea stock grows on shores and new sand dunes without spreading vegetatively. It is seldom seen in the British Isles and was assessed as vulnerable in 2001.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira. It grows in abandoned fields, along roads and in cracks or at the bases of walls and rocks, especially on limestone. It has small rounded white petals and oval seedpods whose stalks eventually spread horizontally.

summary: A mustard-family plant of unstated native origin, found mostly in the Mediterranean region. It closely resembles common shepherd's-purse and is used with Capsella grandiflora to study changes in plant reproduction.

A bulbous flowering plant native from the Balearic Islands through the Mediterranean and western Asia to Tajikistan. It retreats to its bulb in summer, then produces glossy green leaves and deep yellow flowers in autumn. The leaves remain through winter.
Epiphytic climbing plant native to India, China, Southeast Asia and Australia. It has tiny, opposite, lens-shaped leaves and often grows on tree trunks.
A moss of unspecified native origin, it has a cosmopolitan distribution.
A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, it is recorded as introduced in the Azores.

An orchid whose lineage derives from Europe or North Africa, it likely reached the Azores in a single seed migration from mainland Europe. It has exceptionally large flowers compared with the other two Azorean butterfly orchids. Exceptionally rare, it was known from one small upland area of São Jorge when rediscovered, with a flowering specimen later found on Faial.

Orchid endemic to the Azores, where it survives in small, scattered populations in laurisilva scrub across eight islands. This endangered species is a strong indicator of the islands’ remaining semi-natural laurisilva habitats.
A sea-lavender native only to central-western Portugal, where it grows on coastal cliffs and in rocky or sandy places. Its flowers have purplish-red petals.

summary: A waterwort-family plant distributed across Europe and North Africa, it is also recorded in Turkey’s Çanakkale Province. In Portugal it is confined to the far northeast, where it inhabits small permanent ponds and slow-flowing streams and is assessed as Vulnerable.

summary: Flowering plant occurring in North Africa and southwestern Europe. Its two recorded mainland Portuguese subspecies are endemic there: one occurs in west-central Portugal, while the Sintra Mountains subspecies is protected under the Habitats Directive.
Green alga that prefers nutrient-rich environments.

A green seaweed with no native origin specified, thread weed is widespread in the Atlantic and Pacific and lives along coasts from exposed shores to sheltered shallows, tide pools, rocks and sand. It is eaten by humans and animals and is widely produced in China, Japan and Korea.
edibilityNote: The seaweed is edible and widely produced in China, Japan and Korea.

summary: True ginger native to Maritime Southeast Asia. Its beehive-like flower spikes have white, yellow, orange or red bracts that often darken as they mature, surrounding small purple-and-yellow flowers with a papery texture.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in summer-developing meadows on waterlogged or sandy ground beside reservoirs and watercourses, sometimes occupying disturbed areas that flood temporarily.
A herbaceous perennial native to China, Japan, Korea and Siberia, it grows from a short rhizome. At least two varieties are recognized.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in nutrient-enriched meadows beside or within clearings of open pine and holm-oak woods, as well as along roadsides, on lime-rich marl or sandy ground.
A perennial herb, Brazilian woodsorrel has a very long, simple root and tiny stems. Its flowers are yellow or vivid crimson-purple.

An evergreen shrub native to coastal dunes and hills in South Africa’s Western, Eastern and Northern Cape. Its paired, parrot-beak-shaped flowers open bright yellow, turn rusty, and leave dark rusty calyxes that persist after fruiting begins.

An alga widespread in tropical and subtropical regions that infects many trees and shrubs. It typically forms fuzzy, orange-brown spots on leaves and thrives in warm, humid conditions; severe infections can damage foliage and fruit.

A fern found in Australia and New Zealand, the giant maidenhair has striking black stems and triangular fronds divided into rectangular segments. Its underground stem grows unusually deep in the soil.

Evergreen succulent subshrub native and endemic to Gran Canaria. It usually carries a large glossy green rosette on a single unbranched stem, with new rosettes growing from the base. The flowering stem normally dies after producing its yellow flower cluster, usually after about five years.
Flowering succulent endemic to Tenerife in the Canary Islands. It is confined to the island’s north, from Teno Point to the Anaga Peninsula.
Annual herb native to southern Europe, North Africa and the Canary Islands. It is a small, self-supporting grass with simple, broad leaves and has been introduced to Australia.
A flowering plant native to northern Africa and many parts of Europe. It is naturalized in parts of Asia, Africa and Europe.

A large flowering megaherb endemic to New Zealand's subantarctic Auckland and Campbell Islands, Ross lily has fleshy, strap-like dark-green leaves and densely crowded golden-yellow flowers. It favours cold, wet ground and is classified as At Risk—Naturally Uncommon because its range is confined to those island groups.

A flowering sedge occurring across Europe, Central Asia, West Siberia and Xinjiang, China. It favours lowland wetlands on heavy soils near lakes, rivers, reservoirs and coasts, and bears pale-green or orange-brown fruiting structures.

A tussock-forming perennial sedge native to Macaronesia, northwest Africa, much of Europe and Turkey. Its lowest leaf-like bract extends beyond the flower cluster, and its flower spikes appear from March to May. It favours sheltered sea-cliff crevices, salt marshes and coastal river mouths.

A sedge found across Europe and Western and Central Asia, with isolated occurrences in North Africa, greater pond-sedge grows in wet habitats and can dominate swamps. It is Britain’s largest Carex and has glaucous leaves; its closely grouped male spikes help distinguish it from lesser pond-sedge.
An evergreen shrub native to South Africa, it grows 0.7–1.3 metres tall and occurs at elevations of 300–1,400 metres.

An annual succulent herb native to the Mediterranean basin. It produces white flowers during Southern Hemisphere spring, from August to October, and is now also found in southern Australia and New Zealand.

A creeping succulent native to eastern and southern Africa, ranging from Kenya and Angola to South Africa. Its small, faintly toothed leaves have barely visible or absent stalks, while pink-white star-shaped flowers appear in late summer or autumn.

A creeping succulent ground cover indigenous to South Africa’s Eastern Cape, Crassula spathulata grows among leaf litter on rocky ridges, often near forest edges. It has stalked, spoon-shaped leaves with rounded bumps along their edges and tiny pink-white, star-shaped autumn flowers.

A perennial succulent native to southern Africa, particularly the east coast of South Africa. Its long branches trail, climb or hang from rocks and form mats, bearing green or yellow-green leaves often edged red and white or cream star-shaped flowers from winter into spring.

A succulent evergreen subshrub endemic to Southern Africa. It has thick, greyish-teal, sickle-shaped leaves, often marked red and arranged in opposing rows. Dense clusters of brilliant scarlet, pink or nearly white tubular flowers appear in summer.
A sedge native to southern Africa, ranging from Mozambique and Zambia to South Africa.
Bulbous flowering plant originating in South Africa’s Cape Province. Its cultivars flower in late summer or early autumn, most often in bright red, orange or yellow, but occasionally pink or white.
An epiphytic fern native to Japan and eastern Asia. It is deciduous, with brown-scaled rhizomes and finely divided, flat triangular fronds.
An evergreen fern native to Australia and New Zealand. Its fertile fronds form upright clusters, and it has been introduced to the Azores, Madeira and Sri Lanka.
Evergreen shrub or small tree native to Brazil and Uruguay. It has shiny dark-green leaves and pure white flowers that open from tubes and spread in summer.

A tall tree native to Victoria and eastern New South Wales, growing in cool, wet forests and rainforest margins. It has smooth pale bark shed in long ribbons, glossy lance-shaped adult leaves, white flowers and woody cup-shaped to cylindrical fruit.

Deciduous bulbous perennial endemic to South Africa's eastern Cape Provinces and KwaZulu-Natal. Its summer flower spike ranges from white to purple, is topped by leafy bracts like a miniature pineapple, and in most plants has a coconut-like scent.
Climbing, twining flowering plant native to Central Asia. Its dense white or greenish flower clusters develop red floral parts as glossy black fruits form.

summary: Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and assessed as native in Hungary. It inhabits wet meadows, rush beds, marshes and the edges of wetlands and waterways. Easily confused with marsh bedstraw, it is best distinguished when its diagnostic fruits are ripe.

sources.attribution: Raab-Straube E V, Raus T, felipe (2024). Euro + Med-Checklist Notulae, 17. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/g5r5d9 accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Flowering plant whose native origin is not supplied. In Portugal it inhabits wet meadows on sandy soil near the coast.

A small evergreen tree indigenous to Southern Africa, it has glossy foliage on arching, drooping branches. Its orange or purple flowers and fleshy fruit grow directly from the trunk; the fruit is edible but reportedly not very tasty.
edibilityNote: The small, fleshy fruits are edible but reportedly do not taste particularly good.

summary: A hairy perennial flowering plant native to Europe and northern Asia. It forms basal leaf rosettes and solitary lemon-yellow flower heads, while runners can produce new rosettes and dense mats.

An evergreen tree or shrub endemic to New Zealand, narrow-leaved lacebark has a weeping form. Young plants have dense, interlacing branches and small leaves; adults develop narrow, coarsely toothed leaves and bear white flowers from December to February.
A flowering plant native to Eurasia and Morocco in North Africa, it has five-petalled flowers that appear from July to August.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira. It grows in scrub clearings on poor, acidic soils. Downward-rolled leaf margins are reported as a feature needing confirmation.

An evergreen perennial flowering plant from tropical Africa, Congo cockatoo grows in moist, shaded bushland from Cameroon across tropical Africa to Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its bright bird-shaped flowers have long curled nectar spurs; the commonly cultivated ‘African Princess’ clone usually has scarlet-and-yellow flowers.

A deciduous, spreading shrub native to China and Japan. It bears compound dark-green leaves and clusters of light pink or purple, pea-like flowers in summer. Although mainly ornamental, it has also been used to make indigo dye.
A compact succulent shrub native to South Africa. It bears masses of orange to yellow flowers from August to October; the flowers open fully in sunlight.
A flowering plant native to South Africa’s Cape Provinces. This trailing iceplant is sold both in its wild form and as numerous cultivated varieties.

A flowering mint-family plant found across eastern Africa from Sudan to South Africa. It is reasonably resistant to drought and wind, and its bold tubular flowers are larger than those of the similar Leonotis leonurus.

An upright herbaceous perennial occurring across Eurasia, mostly Europe, and North America, this oxeye daisy grows in meadows, along forest edges and roads, and in urban areas. Its conspicuous flower heads combine whitish outer florets with numerous tiny yellow central florets and appear from May to October.

An evergreen shrub native to South Africa and Eswatini, it has glossy dark-green leaves with wavy edges. Profuse pale lilac to lavender, trumpet-shaped flowers marked by deep purple veins appear in spring and early summer.

An ornamental vine native to southern Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia and northern Argentina, Chilean jasmine produces masses of strongly scented white flowers in summer. It becomes deciduous in cool climates and cannot survive freezing.

A perennial grass found across the Mediterranean Basin from Portugal and Morocco to the eastern Mediterranean, it has slender stems and open, nodding flower heads. Their spreading branches carry 7–30 fertile flowering units.

A fern indigenous to the Hawaiian Islands and native across other tropical and subtropical areas, including India and Malaysia. Its coarse, light- to medium-green fronds can exceed three feet, and early Hawaiians used them for hula altars and leis.
edibilityNote: Early Hawaiians reportedly fed young fronds to babies, but the passage does not identify this as food or medicine.

summary: A flowering plant in the borage family, native to mainland Portugal.
A flowering plant recorded in North and South America. It occurs on coastal dunes and sandy shores, cultivated land and market gardens, and around settlements.

sources.title: Oenothera indecora Cambess.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree native to eastern Asia, specifically central and southern Japan and Taiwan, holly olive bears very fragrant white flowers in autumn. Spiny leaves predominate on young plants, while unspined leaves predominate higher on mature plants; dark purple fruit ripens the following summer.

Evergreen flowering shrub or small tree native to southern Africa, from South Africa and Lesotho to Mozambique and Zimbabwe. It has showy bright yellow flowers and berry-like fruits that darken to brown or black around a pale, bone-coloured seed. Most varieties have woolly, dull, toothed oval leaves, while the rotundatum variety has glossy, round leaves.

A succulent subshrub native to the Solomon Islands, New Caledonia, Norfolk Island, the southwestern Pacific and warmer parts of New Zealand, where its South Island range is limited to specified northwestern areas. It grows on forest floors and occasionally as a low trunk epiphyte.
Flowering plant native to South Africa and Eswatini. Its foliage resembles that of Coleus; the ornamental cultivar ‘Easy Gold’ is especially noted for this feature.
A flowering grass native to Portugal's Madeira Archipelago.

A perennial native to the Himalayas, Assam, Myanmar, and south-central and southeastern China. It usually has purple flowers, though red, white and bright-pink forms occur, together with hairy, pale-green leaves.

An erect annual or short-lived perennial herb native to Australia; its status in parts of New Zealand is uncertain. It has a bristly main stem, narrow lobed lower leaves and many small yellow or pale-yellow flower heads.

A perennial flowering herb native to central and eastern Russia, Kazakhstan, Mongolia and northwestern China, Maltese-cross has unbranched stems and opposite leaves. It bears clusters of bright red flowers with deeply cleft lobes forming a Maltese-cross shape; cultivated varieties may instead be orange-red, pink or white.
A flowering plant native to Algeria, Morocco, Portugal, Spain and Tunisia. It mainly grows in subtropical regions and was introduced to Corsica in 1967.
A bulb-forming perennial native to Cape Province in South Africa. It bears white to cream flowers and grows in sandy, waterlogged soils.

Flowering shrub native to southern Africa, with sticky, aromatic, heart-shaped leaves that smell of ginger when crushed. Its abundant white, lilac or pink flowers form large clusters at the ends of otherwise bare branches in winter in subtropical or temperate climates.
Perennial climbing vine native across South and Southeast Asia. It has tuberous roots and produces red tubular flowers from January to April.

A flowering plant native to an area extending from southeastern Brazil to northeastern Argentina. Its pink-tipped white flowers and green-purple foliage make it attractive to gardeners, but it can become invasive where grown as an ornamental.
A tuber-growing plant native to the south-southwestern and southern Cape Provinces. It grows mainly in subtropical environments.
