summary: A flowering plant whose native origin is not given, the spotted calla lily has slender, pointed leaves attractively speckled with white. Its flowers have a white, funnel-shaped outer part surrounding a yellowish centre.
A flowering parasitic plant found in Madeira, where it is introduced. It attacks various herbs and shrubs in dry, sunny, low-altitude sites.

A small to medium-sized tree endemic to New South Wales, Australia. It has thick, rough fibrous bark, narrow greyish-green adult leaves, white flowers and small woody fruit; fewer than 40 localities are known.
An evergreen shrub or small tree endemic to New Zealand. It commonly grows on another plant and sends grooved roots toward the forest floor, and it has large, thick, glossy leaves.

A moss of unstated native origin, recorded across Europe, Asia, the Americas, Africa, Australia and Antarctica. It forms loose brown-green mats; dry shoots look dark brown and bud-like, while wet upper leaves spread into rosettes. In Europe only female plants have been found, and spore capsules are known only from Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand.

A herbaceous perennial endemic to New Zealand, naturally occurring near the sea on rocks north of Greymouth and Kaikōura. Its tall flower stalk bears many white flowers with purple, white and yellow stamens. Māori historically ate its rhizomes after cooking them in a hāngī.
edibilityNote: Rhizomes are edible when cooked and were historically cooked in a hāngī and eaten by Māori.

summary: A shrub endemic to New Zealand, shrubby tororaro has small, heart-shaped leaves among wiry, interlocking branches. It is usually leafless in winter and forms a dense, tangled shape.

Perennial or biennial plant endemic to Europe, though absent from Finland and Eastern Europe, with small populations in European Turkey and Svalbard. Young plants form ground-level rosettes before producing taller shoots bearing many bright yellow flower heads, typically in damp, grazed or disturbed grassland.
An evergreen or semi-evergreen shrub native to East Asia. Its flowers range from white to dark red, and some varieties are poisonous because they contain grayanotoxin.

Herbaceous perennial native to Chile and Argentina, with brittle, fleshy roots and erect, narrow-leaved stems. Its orchid-like yellow or orange flowers appear in early to midsummer and may be heavily spotted or striped with red or brown.

A bulbous plant native to South Africa, this frost-resistant evergreen perennial grows in the Drakensberg grasslands. Its rust-coloured stems carry cream to coral-pink flowers that turn yellow from late summer into mid-autumn, above narrow blue-green leaves.
A cactus native to Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, it can form more than 100 jointed stem segments. It is considered invasive in Africa and Australia.

A woody climbing vine native to woodlands in Japan, the Korean peninsula and Sakhalin. It climbs with small aerial roots and produces flat summer flower clusters with peripheral sterile white flowers around numerous fertile off-white flowers. Its young leaves are edible when cooked and are sometimes added to miso in Japan.
edibilityNote: Young leaves are eaten cooked, sometimes in Japanese miso, and are described as tasting like cucumber.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to New Zealand’s Chatham Islands. It is grown as a garden tree and used for firewood, including in other mild oceanic climates such as Scotland.

A large upright shrub or small tree native to South Africa, the oleander-leaf protea has green or blue-grey leaves that curve upward directly from its stems. Its cone-like flower heads have pink, carmine, creamy-green or whitish outer bracts, typically edged with a distinctive hairy black fringe.
A flowering shrub or small tree found from the central Himalayas to northern Indo-China. It has pointed, ribbed leaves and clusters of fragrant, pale pink flowers in autumn and winter.
Bromeliad endemic to southern Brazil, commonly grown as an ornamental plant. Recognized varieties occur from São Paulo south to Rio Grande do Sul, with one reported specifically from Santa Catarina.
A flowering bromeliad native to the Atlantic Forest of southern Brazil and Misiones province in eastern Argentina.
A succulent perennial endemic to eastern Australia, the giant spear lily forms a rosette of long, sword-shaped leaves. In spring, its flowers rise on a very tall stalk.

A low-growing evergreen shrub native to China, Afghanistan, northeastern India, Bhutan and Nepal. It bears fragrant white flowers throughout winter, followed by black berries; its varieties can differ greatly in appearance.

A deciduous flowering shrub native to northeastern Asia. Its three-lobed, maple-like leaves often turn red in autumn; flat white flower heads appear in early summer, followed by round red berries in autumn.

An evergreen shrub found in the high Andean Yungas valleys of western South America, it bears clusters of brilliant pink, narrow tubular flowers in early spring. It is Peru’s national flower and one of Bolivia’s two national flowers.

Evergreen flowering shrub native to Nepal, the eastern Himalaya, Assam, Myanmar, Vietnam, Tibet, and central and southern China, but not Taiwan. Its leaves emerge red in early spring before turning green, while clusters of creamy-white flowers open alongside the young leaves.

An evergreen terrestrial bromeliad endemic to central Chile. It forms dense rosettes of grey-green leaves armed with hooked spines, while its green or yellow flower spikes resemble medieval maces. Growth is slow, and flowering may take 20 years or more.
Bromeliad native to Brazil, northern Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay and Uruguay. It is typical of Brazil’s Cerrado vegetation and is often grown as an ornamental.

Deciduous tree native to the Caucasus, Kaçkar and Alborz mountains of eastern Europe and southwest Asia. It has a distinctive vase-shaped crown, with a short, broad trunk splitting low into many nearly upright branches, and small greenish flowers without petals.

An evergreen subshrub native to Argentina and Chile, bush slipperwort has highly veined, slightly sticky, puckered leaves. Clusters of lemon-yellow, snapdragon-shaped flowers appear throughout spring and summer.

Groundcover violet native to Australia's east coast from near Brisbane to Batemans Bay. It has striking purple-and-white flowers and bright-green, nearly circular mature leaves with a deep, narrow V-shaped notch at the base.

A bulbous perennial native to Southern Africa, it grows across the region’s winter-rainfall zone in fynbos and renosterveld. Its red flower heads appear before the broad, strap-shaped leaves and are followed by translucent white-to-red fleshy berries.

A large evergreen shrub native to Tibet and south-central China, late cotoneaster bears clusters of white flowers followed by masses of small red fruit in autumn. Birds unusually avoid the fruit, which can remain on the plant through winter.

A compact evergreen shrub reported native to Ireland, southwestern France, Spain, Portugal and Tangier, though its isolated Irish occurrence may be a garden escape. Its brittle foliage stays green, and deep pink, honey-scented flowers open in winter and spring.

Tree or shrub native to French Polynesia, the Cook Islands and the Pitcairn Islands. It commonly forms part of the canopy in montane and cloud forests, sometimes becoming a shrub on windswept mountaintops.

A spreading shrub or tree endemic to New Zealand, rawirinui is widespread on the North and South Islands, mainly near coasts, lowlands and forest margins. Its rough bark peels upward in long strips, and its small white flowers form compact groups.
Perennial cactus native to Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina. It has fleshy, cylindrical, trailing stems and white flowers.
A shrub endemic to southeastern Australia. Its gland-dotted, oblong to egg-shaped leaves accompany white to pink flowers borne singly or in small groups from the leaf axils.

A perennial herb endemic to the western Mediterranean Basin. Its saxophone-shaped flowers lure small flies, temporarily trapping them before releasing them with pollen. Long-term consumption of its roots or rhizomes can cause irreversible kidney damage, and their aristolochic acids may be carcinogenic when taken internally.
edibilityNote: Roots or rhizomes consumed over long periods can cause irreversible kidney damage; internal aristolochic acids may be carcinogenic.

summary: Plant species in the nettle family; its native origin is not specified.

A large deciduous tree common on the plains and lower hills of South and Southeast Asia. Its leaves crowd toward branch tips, and its rounded nuts have five flatter sides. The kernels are eaten by the Lodha people of the Indian subcontinent for their mind-altering qualities.
edibilityNote: The Lodha people of the Indian subcontinent eat the kernels for their mind-altering qualities.

summary: Flowering bromeliad native to Brazil. Its robust, sharp-edged leaves form a vase-like rosette whose funnels often collect water. It bears long-lasting flower heads with striking pink bracts and blue petals that turn red and white as they wilt.

An erect shrub or small tree native to the southwest coast of Western Australia, it has prominent red-and-white flower spikes, mainly in spring. Fire kills the plant but opens seed-storing pods, allowing it to regenerate from seed.
A slowly spreading evergreen perennial native to northern Iran. It has oval, hairy leaves and bright yellow, spurred flowers in late spring and early summer.

Flowering plant in the rose family endemic to southwestern continental Europe. In Portugal it occurs only in rocky habitats above 1,800 metres on Serra da Estrela’s upper plateau; a 2020 mainland assessment classified it as Critically Endangered there.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A deciduous shrub native to China and Japan, it bears yellow flowers marked with dark red flecks. Though rarely cultivated, it is a parent of many yellow-flowered hybrids.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows along the edges and in clearings of deciduous woodland, and also colonizes roadside banks and rocky outcrops in forest settings. It is protected under Annexes II and IV of the Habitats Directive.

A prickly shrub native to eastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland, Australia. Its crowded, stiff leaves accompany spider-like flower heads in red, pink, orange, yellow or greenish shades. Bushfires kill the plants, which regenerate afterward from seed.
An annual or biennial herb native to parts of Europe and western Asia. It grows in grassland, disturbed ground and roadsides, and its tough taproot can make it difficult to remove from gardens.
edibilityNote: Leaves and seeds are eaten in salads; the source also records use as famine food.

summary: A cactus native to central and eastern Brazil. It develops a woody trunk and large crown, while its white flowers open at dusk and last only one night.

Rainforest tree native to eastern Australia, where it grows along streams from New South Wales to central eastern Queensland. It has thin, wavy-edged leaves and produces white summer flowers followed by pale pink or greenish berries.
A shrub endemic to South Africa, it has grey to bluish-green leaves with hard margins. Its woody fruits remain on the plant, and seeds are released from dry flower heads after wildfire.

A perennial herb native to Europe and North Africa, including most Mediterranean islands. Its basal, round-toothed leaves accompany one or two scented yellow flowers, which appear from October to December and may cover large areas.

An evergreen twining vine native to the Portuguese island of Madeira. Deep pink buds open into fragrant, white, star-shaped summer flowers, and the species is critically endangered in its native range.

An evergreen shrub or tree with aromatic, glossy dark-green leaves, native to Madeira and the Canary Islands. It grows in humid cloud-zone forests and bears male and female flowers on separate plants.

A flowering plant introduced in mainland Portugal, the Azores and Madeira; its native origin is not stated. It is naturalized in fields and dunes, especially disturbed coastal sites with sandy, nitrogen-enriched soil.

An evergreen succulent vine native to South Africa, Eswatini and Zimbabwe, it trails for several metres and bears heart-shaped leaves. Older plants develop a woody base, while tubers often form on the roots and sometimes along the stems, creating its rosary-like appearance.
An evergreen shrub native to Madeira. It is rare there, growing on exposed coastal and inland rocky slopes, and has separate male and female plants with similar flower clusters.
A fern native to Madeira, where it grows in subtropical moist lowland forest. It is threatened by habitat loss.
Flowering plant endemic to Madeira, Portugal. It is protected under Portuguese or European legislation, including the Habitats Directive and the Convention on European Wildlife and Natural Habitats.
A flowering plant endemic to Madeira, Sedum brissemoretii grows on the island’s coastal sea cliffs. It is protected under Annex II of the Habitats Directive.
Flowering plant endemic to Madeira and belonging to the mustard family.
A flowering plant in the mustard family, Sinapidendron frutescens has two listed subspecies, both endemic to Madeira.
A flowering plant endemic to Portugal's Madeira archipelago. It is protected under Portuguese or European legislation, including Annexes II and IV of the Habitats Directive.
A flowering plant endemic to Madeira, Portugal, Sinapidendron gymnocalyx belongs to the mustard family.
A rowan species endemic to Madeira, Sorbus maderensis is threatened by habitat loss.
Flowering plant endemic to Portugal's Madeira Archipelago.
A flowering plant endemic to Madeira.
A flowering plant whose subspecies Chaenorhinum serpyllifolium subsp. lusitanicum is endemic to mainland Portugal. That subspecies is protected under Portuguese and European Union law.

Flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and Portugal's Berlengas archipelago, growing in dry fields, paths and disturbed ground. The Iberian subspecies is annual, while the Berlengas subspecies is described as biannual or perennial; both have highly branched stems and dense flower clusters.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows on coastal sands, mainly primary dunes and openings in secondary-dune scrub, including somewhat disturbed sites.
A prostrate to ascending perennial herb endemic to eastern Australia, white fanflower has pale blue or white fan-shaped flowers and bright green, slightly hairy leaves with smooth or toothed edges.
Shrub or tree endemic to Madagascar, it is widespread across the island. It grows in habitats ranging from humid coastal and lowland forests to dry deciduous and montane forests.
An orchid occurring in southern Brazil, northeastern Argentina and Paraguay, and reported from eastern Peru.

Terrestrial slipper orchid native to the Khasi Hills of Assam and Meghalaya and adjoining Sylhet in Bangladesh, where it may now be extinct; it is also reported from northwest Yunnan. It bears one large, variably coloured flower with a helmet-shaped lip and is very rare in the wild.
A succulent plant native to South Africa, it is also known as the pickle plant.
Succulent endemic to South Africa’s southern Cape Provinces around Makhanda. It forms clumps of fleshy triangular leaves and produces yellow, daisy-like flowers in autumn.
A perennial herb of unspecified native origin, it is recorded in Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia and Brazil. It is grown in gardens for its flowers and blooms profusely in late summer.
A rare annual flowering plant endemic to southern Portugal, especially inland Alentejo. It has thick, linear leaves with slightly curled tips and small violet flowers, blooming from February to June.

summary: A mustard-family flowering plant endemic to the central and northern mountains of mainland Portugal, it grows in rock cracks, cliffs and path embankments, mainly on siliceous rock such as schist.

A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it has a very restricted mainland Portuguese range in the Algarve between Algoz and Faro. It grows in sparse grassland on iron-rich clay soils that flood temporarily in winter and early spring, and its Portuguese population is assessed as Endangered amid continuing habitat and population decline.

summary: Coastal plant endemic to southwestern mainland Portugal, growing on consolidated sandy cliff soils with some iron and surface moisture. In the 2016–2019 assessment, only three subpopulations were known, two created by reintroduction at historical sites, while habitat and population declines continued.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to mainland Portugal, Silene rothmaleri is protected as a priority species under European habitat and wildlife agreements.

A flowering subshrub endemic to southwest Portugal, especially coastal heath and scrub on stabilized limestone-sand dunes. It has pink or purple flowers, often pale pink or reddish bracts, and leaves densely dotted with yellowish glands.

A flowering plant endemic to central Algarve in southern Portugal. It grows both on the coast, in pine clearings and dry scrub on sandy acidic ground, and inland, in thyme vegetation and scrub clearings on marginal or calcareous ground.
A small epiphytic orchid found in Madagascar’s humid evergreen forests. It has leathery, wavy-edged leaves and produces hanging clusters of large pure-white flowers that open successively in autumn.

A flowering plant endemic to southwestern Portugal between Setúbal and Sines. It grows in scrub on stabilized dunes, sometimes beneath pine forests, and can become abundant in disturbed areas with acidic sandy soil.

A robust perennial herb endemic to mainland Portugal, restricted to fragmented populations in the country's west. It grows in heath, gorse scrub and pinewoods on somewhat moist sandy soils, and was assessed as Vulnerable for mainland Portugal during 2016–2019 amid continuing decline.

summary: An aquatic flowering plant native to the Azores. A 2020 mainland Portugal assessment found its historical distribution uncertain because of repeated confusion with a similar species; it was then known only from Algarve and Baixo Alentejo and assessed as Vulnerable.

summary: A dandelion endemic to Portugal's Monchique range. Its current presence is known only around Foia, and the mainland Portuguese assessment classifies it as Vulnerable because of its very small occupied area and single known location.

summary: Plant endemic to southwestern mainland Portugal, growing in scrub clearings on sandy soils. Its current distribution and population are highly uncertain because it has repeatedly been confused with a close relative; seven locations are identified, and suitable habitat has declined in recent decades.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: Flowering plant native to Portugal, Spain and France. Its 'Grace Ward' and 'Heavenly Blue' cultivars have received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

A flowering shrub or small tree native to northern Vietnam, southern China, Hainan, Taiwan, the Ryukyu Islands and southern Kyushu. It is grown in hedges, containers and bonsai, and serves as a street tree in several southern Chinese cities.

A flowering plant endemic to southern mainland Portugal and restricted to the Algarve’s Barrocal. It grows along edges and clearings of lime-loving scrub and was assessed as Vulnerable in the 2020 mainland Portugal Red List, with only six or seven current locations identified.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A shrub endemic to Cape Verde, where it grows on rocky ground and escarpments across several climate zones. It has milky sap, elliptical leaves arranged in rosettes and yellow flowers.
A flowering plant native to Southern Africa, Ceropegia linearis has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

A tree native to Indochina, southern India and parts of Malesia, sea fig can begin life growing on another plant and later develop a strangling habit. This is not obligatory, and it also grows as a single-stemmed forest tree.
A climbing shrub widespread in South-East Asia and Australoceania, Salacia chinensis has yellow or yellowish-green flowers with five petals. Its fruit contains a single seed.

Tree-like aloe indigenous to southern Africa. Its thin, recurved pale-green leaves form a distinctive spiral and have many small pink-white marginal teeth; its cone-shaped flower clusters are pink or dull scarlet.

A flowering plant endemic to central Portugal, it inhabits scrub clearings on rocky slopes exposed to Atlantic influence. During mainland Portugal's 2016–2019 assessment, it was classed as Endangered, with an estimated 350–370 mature plants and uncertainty over whether two historical populations had disappeared.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Arabis beirana
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: Stemless thistle endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in scrub clearings and traditional dry olive groves on basic, non-calcareous soils. A 2016–2019 mainland Portuguese assessment classified it as Vulnerable, with most populations small and isolated and intensive irrigated olive farming its gravest threat.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, Cynara algarbiensis occurs in southern Portugal and southwestern Spain. It belongs to the artichoke genus.

Perennial grass native to Australia, New Zealand, New Caledonia and Tonga. Its horizontal runners spread across coastal dunes and bind loose sand. Mature female seed heads detach and roll like tumbleweeds.

Evergreen shrub from the southern mountains and coastal provinces of South Africa. Its lower branches are uniquely covered in pustules, while its wedge-shaped leaves and yellow flower heads that turn orange create a pincushion effect with their long projecting styles. After fire kills the growth above ground, multiple branches can sprout from its woody rootstock.

A flowering plant native to Central and South America, the friendship plant is bushy and trailing, with bright green, quilted leaves that often have bronze or reddish undersides. Its small pink-white flowers appear infrequently indoors, and it is primarily grown as a houseplant.

A shrub or tree from southern Africa, mainly South Africa and neighbouring countries. Usually evergreen, it grows as a shrub in dry areas but can become a tree where water is sufficient. Its leathery brown pods contain smooth seeds, each bearing a yellowish cup-shaped covering.
edibilityNote: The seeds are edible; no preparation or historical context is given.

summary: A rainforest plant native to Brazil. Commonly grown indoors in temperate climates, it is valued for striking variegated leaves with purple undersides. Outdoors it suits humid tropical conditions but needs afternoon shade and protection from high winds.

A climbing plant native to Southeast Asia, including southern China, mainland Indochina and Java, heart hoya has thick, heart-shaped leaves. Mature plants bear clusters of flowers that produce red-to-brown nectar droplets and release their scent at night.
Bulb-forming perennial native to the Caribbean islands and northern South America. It bears striking white flowers in clusters, with narrow flower parts that usually droop while blooming.

A terrestrial orchid native to humid forests of southern China, northeastern India, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia and Myanmar. Its velvety wine-red to dark-green leaves are striped, with pink undersides, while annual late-winter to early-spring spikes carry many small white flowers.

A tree or tall shrub endemic to Australia, growing along streams and swampy flats in southeastern Queensland and northern New South Wales. It has whitish papery bark, narrow oil-rich leaves and short-lived, fluffy masses of white or cream flowers.
edibilityNote: Tea tree oil is toxic if swallowed and can cause serious effects, including coma.

summary: A tree native to moist regions of southern, eastern and central tropical Africa, the forest elder has a crooked trunk with rough, flaking bark and a rounded crown. From autumn to spring, it produces large clusters of small, sweetly scented white or cream flowers.
A deciduous, nitrogen-fixing shrub found in India, China, Taiwan and other parts of Asia. Its leaves and roots are used as an insecticide.
A mound-forming evergreen perennial native to Brazil. It has corrugated, heart-shaped leaves and narrow spikes of white flowers in summer, and is popular as a houseplant.

A perennial subshrub native from central South America to central Argentina and the Río de la Plata coast, Bonpland's croton has a copper-coloured woody stem base and many branches. It favours disturbed sandy soils and is sometimes a highly invasive weed.

Tropical flowering plant native to woodlands of North, Central and South America, especially Brazil's Atlantic Forest. It resembles ginger but is related to spiderworts, with spotted stems, large glossy horizontal leaves and striking blue flowers.
An Asian tropical-forest understory shrub recorded from southern China to Indochina. It has red tubers, green flowers and black berries.
Tree native to Brazil. It is pollinated by hummingbirds and is often cultivated, with introduced populations in Africa and India.

A succulent plant with an obscure wild origin, antique spurge is widespread in peninsular India and cultivated or naturalized across many tropical regions. Its juice has been used as a potent ingredient in wall plaster, and its trade is regulated under CITES Appendix II.
A shrub native to eastern Southeast Asia, New Guinea and Australia. It has arching branches, tiny linear leaves and solitary white flowers, and is popular for bonsai.

A rhizomatous perennial begonia native to southern China and northern Vietnam. Its large, asymmetrical green leaves are textured, reddish-haired and marked centrally with a prominent dark brown cross-like pattern. The small white flowers are less valued in cultivation than the foliage.
A small to medium deciduous tree native to southern and tropical Africa. Its fragrant blue-mauve flowers hang in clusters that may cover the tree, followed by brown pods that remain closed.
A rainforest tree native to eastern Australia, lacebark grows in drier rainforest areas. It has pink flowers without petals, lobed leaves that are whitish underneath, and hairy, boat-shaped fruits.
edibilityNote: The seeds are edible to humans when roasted.

summary: A small flowering shrub native to southern Africa, including South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini, wild kopieva has low rooting stems and slender, upright succulent leaves. Its orange, yellow or white flowers have distinctive tufts on their stamens.
Tree native to southern Africa, with an isolated population in eastern Zimbabwe. It bears abundant sprays of bright yellow flowers and thin, papery, straw-coloured pods.

A deciduous tree native to Asia, with separate male and female trees. Its fruit has sour, edible white pulp surrounding a hard, olive-sized seed. In Nepal, the pulp is traditionally made into pickles, sweets, spices and other sour foods.
edibilityNote: The sour white fruit pulp is edible and traditionally used in Nepal for pickles, sweets, spices and other foods.

summary: A twining evergreen climber native to tropical Western Africa. It produces clusters of brilliant scarlet flowers in summer.

Pseudobulbous epiphytic orchid native from peninsular Thailand to western Malesia. It grows on trees in wet tropical mountain forest and bears hanging clusters of short-lived, pleasantly fragrant, greenish-white flowers with a white-and-purple-red patterned lip.

sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A poisonous bulb-forming climber of unspecified native origin, found across southern and eastern Africa. Its leaves are largely reduced, and what resembles a climbing stem is actually a succulent, highly branched flower cluster arising from the bulb.
edibilityNote: Ingesting a concentrated decoction can rapidly cause fatal poisoning; the bulb and above-ground parts are especially toxic.

summary: A perennial succulent endemic to South Africa’s Eastern Cape. Its short upright branches bear fine aerial roots and green-to-grey, wavy-edged leaves; in spring it sends up long stalks of white tubular flowers tinged with red.

Flowering tree native to southern China, Vietnam, Japan, Korea and Taiwan. New leaves tend to be red before becoming green, and its small cream to light-pink flowers are followed by dark blue to black, olive-shaped fruit.
edibilityNote: The fruit is explicitly described as inedible.

summary: A flowering plant widespread across tropical Africa, Asia and Australia.

Evergreen tree native to the subtropical mountains of southern China and Taiwan. It has glossy, feathery foliage and fragrant white trumpet-shaped flowers that open at night and wilt the following morning.

A herbaceous perennial native to Southeastern Europe, including much of the Balkan Peninsula and nearby parts of Romania and Turkey. Slender upright stems carry deep red pincushion-like flowers through summer, although lilac and pink forms also occur; its basal leaves are typically withered by flowering time.

A deciduous scrambling shrub native from Europe to the Caucasus and northwestern Africa. It has long curved thorns and fragrant pink flowers, followed by soft hips rich in vitamin C. In Turkey, the hips have traditionally been made into marmalade, syrup, jam, tea and jelly.
edibilityNote: In Turkey, the hips have traditionally been collected in winter and processed into marmalade, syrup, jam, tea and jelly.

summary: A green alga with a North Pacific distribution from the Gulf of Alaska to central California, it forms frayed, rope-like strands as hooked branches entangle neighbouring growth. It occurs on intertidal rocks in protected to semi-exposed places during spring and early summer.
A flowering plant native to the southwestern Cape Provinces of South Africa, this species may be a parent of the cultivated regal pelargonium.

Epiphytic moss occurring in Europe, parts of North Africa and Asia, and the Azores. It forms dark-green mats, and its folded, veinless leaves lie close when dry but rapidly unfold with moisture; spore capsules are extremely rare.

summary: A flowering tree native to Cuba, Jamaica, the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico, blue mahoe has broad green leaves and flowers that change from bright yellow through orange and red to crimson as they mature. Its polished wood is distinctive for its blue-green streaks.
Herbaceous perennial native to Brazil. Its sage-scented dark green leaves and crowded orange-red flowers are set among velvety red-brown hairs on young stems and flower clusters.

An evergreen flowering shrub native to Mozambique, Eswatini and several South African provinces. It has rounded, hairy leaves and summer spikes of soft blue or mauve flowers, and commonly grows in the moist, dappled shade of forest margins.
A perennial grass native to northeastern Africa and parts of the Arabian Peninsula. It forms spreading clumps and has flower heads surrounded by a cloudlike mass of feathery white bristles.

Perennial bunch grass native to open, scrubby habitats in East Africa, tropical Africa, the Middle East and southwestern Asia. It is fast-growing and drought-tolerant, with numerous feathery purple flower spikes, and has become invasive in some introduced regions.

A shrub of unstated native origin, widespread in southern and central Africa. It contains potentially deadly cardiac glycosides and has been used for arrow poison. Only fully ripe fruit is sweet and edible; unripe fruit and all other parts are poisonous.
edibilityNote: Only fully ripe fruit is eaten; unripe fruit and all other plant parts are poisonous.

summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree native to Mozambique and South Africa, it grows in dry forest and coastal thickets. It has fragrant white flowers tinged with pink and purple berries when ripe. The plant has been used as arrow poison.

A vine-like plant native to the humid tropics from the Malay Peninsula south to Java. It grows on trees or rocks, with leathery green leaves and usually scarlet tubular flowers with yellow throats; it also has a pungent smell.

A tree-like aloe indigenous to South Africa’s Eastern Cape, it bears orange or yellow flowers from winter to early spring. Each flower bends upward, sometimes almost at a right angle, and the narrow, recurved leaves form a relatively untidy rosette.
Tree-growing rainforest plant native to Costa Rica. Its most memorable feature is a curled orange-red flower spike, accompanied by shiny, spear-shaped leaves.
A daisy-family plant endemic to Fuerteventura in the Canary Islands. It has since been introduced to other islands in the archipelago.
An orchid native to Brazil.

A shrub or small tree of unspecified native origin, southern raintree is recorded in parts of Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina and Uruguay. Its terminal clusters contain fragrant flowers, while its nearly spherical or egg-shaped capsules hold numerous dark brown seeds.

A thorny shrub native to central-eastern Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil. It grows slowly and has flattened, grey-green, spine-like branches with fragrant white tubular flowers grouped in the leaf joints.
An evergreen perennial endemic to Somalia in East Africa. It has hairy, slightly succulent leaves and three-lobed blue or purple summer flowers.

A fast-growing shrub or small tree endemic to Argentina and Bolivia, it has heart-shaped leaves with a distinctive pungent smell. Its berries turn yellow-orange when ripe; ripe fruit is edible but may taste unpredictable or unpleasant, while unripe berries are mildly toxic.
edibilityNote: Ripe fruits are edible; unripe berries are mildly toxic, and flavor can be unpredictable or unpleasant.

summary: A variable shrub or multi-stemmed tree native to seasonally dry tropical Africa. Its fibre is used for ropes and baskets, its wood for bows and tool handles, and its pith is edible.
edibilityNote: The pith is eaten; no preparation or historical context is specified.

summary: A bushy shrublet indigenous to South Africa, including the Western and Eastern Cape and Namaqualand. Its fragrant, softly felted foliage looks silvery, while snowy-white petals can nearly cover the flowering bush.
edibilityNote: The plant has been used in cooking, but the source does not identify the parts or preparation.

summary: A deciduous bulbous perennial native to Malawi, Zimbabwe and southern Africa. In mid to late summer, a stem rises from wavy-edged leaves, carrying green, yellow or white flowers beneath a head of green leaflike bracts. Its scented flowers and later fruiting stems remain decorative for many weeks.
A plant native to Brazil, especially Paraná, Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina and São Paulo. It flowers from August to December and bears edible yellow fruit called uvalha from September to January.
edibilityNote: The yellow fruit, called uvalha, is edible and is produced between September and January.

summary: A succulent endemic to South Africa, particularly the east-central and southeastern Cape Provinces and southern KwaZulu-Natal. It has snake-like horizontal branches, a swollen underground stem, photosynthetic modified stems and needle-like leaves.

A perennial grass native to France, Italy, Spain and Switzerland. Its fine blue-grey blades form compact, porcupine-like domes, followed in late spring or early summer by pale green, purple-tinged flowers and puffy, wheat-like seed heads.
An ornamental fig plant native to Vanuatu in the South Pacific, the mosaic fig produces fruit directly from its main stems or woody trunks rather than from new shoots.

An evergreen shrub or climbing plant endemic to southeastern and southern Brazil, Fuchsia regia inhabits high-altitude Atlantic Forest, often near water in shade. Its slender wine-purple branches bear hanging flowers with red tubes and violet-fuchsia petals, followed by dark-purple berries.

A wild perennial shrub native to semi-arid southern Africa and the region from Syria to Afghanistan. Its small yellow flowers have purple centres, while ripe capsules burst open to reveal short cotton fibres firmly attached to the seeds.
edibilityNote: In the Levant, seeds were used as food or for oil; human consumption requires heating or another treatment to remove toxic gossypol.

summary: An evergreen bulbous perennial native to the coast and mountains of South Africa. Its partly exposed bright-green bulb produces broad leaves, brush-like clusters of tiny white flowers in late autumn and winter, and fleshy red fruits.

A shrub occurring mainly in southern Ecuador and adjacent Peru, with isolated records farther north in Ecuador. It bears clusters of deep-purple tubular flowers and produces conical berries whose lower third is enclosed by the flower cup.

A tall, corm-forming plant from around Tulbagh in South Africa’s Cape Province. Its rare turquoise, star-shaped flowers have black-purple centres and grow in long clusters; the plant is considered vulnerable as its habitat is often destroyed by human activity.
Evergreen flowering shrub indigenous to South Africa. It has scrambling growth, pinnate leaves and masses of strongly scented, star-shaped white flowers that attract various birds.
A shrub native to Afghanistan, the Indian subcontinent, Laos, Myanmar and Vietnam. It has bitter, opposite leaves, usually white flowers in dense spikes, and hairy, club-shaped fruit capsules.

A flowering plant native to northeastern South Africa, Eswatini, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. Compared with the similar Kalanchoe thyrsiflora, it has larger, more vibrant leaves and unscented white flowers.
A flowering succulent subshrub native to Madagascar, the flour-dust plant has arching stems with fleshy leaves coated in fine, mealy white wax and clusters of purple-veined pink flowers in spring.

A large evergreen shrub endemic to the southern coast of South Africa’s Western Cape. Its large, rounded leaves have several deep teeth, while long orange styles curve inward from orange flower heads to create a pincushion appearance. It grows chiefly on coastal limestone ridges.

An evergreen trailing shrub endemic to Spain’s Canary Islands, parrot’s beak may be extinct in the wild or survive there only as a few individuals. It has fine, silvery foliage and orange-red to red flowers shaped like upward-facing beaks.
An evergreen shrub native to China, it grows at high elevations. Its flowers may be white, pink or pale red.
An evergreen tree native to eastern Africa, it bears clusters of large, bright yellow trumpet-shaped flowers with orange-red markings in the throat. Its long fruit capsules contain many winged seeds.

A densely branched shrub native to South Australia and parts of Victoria. Its leaves grow in alternating right-angled pairs, forming four rows along the stems. Pink or purple flower spikes rapidly fade to white, followed by woody capsules fused at their bases and sunken into the stems.
A flowering plant native to South America, including northern Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia and southern Brazil. It has been introduced to Portugal, including the Azores and Madeira.

A leafless succulent perennial native to the coastal belt of South Africa's Western Cape. Its cactus-like toothed stems form clumps, while its highly variable star-shaped flowers are off-white or yellow, heavily speckled with maroon and sometimes faintly carrion-scented.

Evergreen shrub or small tree native to South America, specifically Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil. It has leathery, alternating leaves with up to 57 leaflets and hanging reddish-brown flower clusters with a sour smell that are active mainly at night.

A broadleaf evergreen shrub native to China and Tibet, Chinese pittosporum has densely packed green foliage and fragrant white to yellow flowers in spring. It is commonly grown as an ornamental hedge or screen in temperate gardens.
A flowering plant native to China, the Indian subcontinent and Indochina. Compounds extracted from its dried leaves and stems have shown activity against one malaria parasite.

A perennial deciduous woody vine native to forests of northern China, the Russian Far East, Korea and Japan, it produces smooth red berries in dense hanging clusters. Its crushed leaves smell lemony and can be eaten as a vegetable, while Koreans make the berries into a cordial drink called omija-cha.
edibilityNote: The leaves are used as a vegetable, and Koreans make the berries into the cordial drink omija-cha.

summary: A perennial herb native to Angola, Mozambique, Swaziland, Zambia, Zimbabwe and parts of South Africa, coral ragwort has a soft stem and succulent leaves. Its oval leaves narrow toward the base and have prominent pointed teeth.
A shrub native to northeastern Argentina, southeastern and southern Brazil, and Uruguay, this species belongs to the nightshade family.

A fruiting plant with no stated native origin, Ethiopian eggplant is mainly found in Asia and tropical Africa. Its highly variable fruit can resemble both eggplant and tomato, turning bright red when mature. The fruit is eaten raw or cooked, usually while green, and ranges from sweet to very bitter; the leaves are also eaten.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten as a vegetable; fruit is eaten raw or cooked, usually harvested green, with sweetness and bitterness varying by variety.

summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree native to open woodland in South Africa and Madagascar. It has large pale-green leaves and clusters of white flowers with red and yellow stamens that move rapidly when touched.
A rapidly growing perennial vine native to West Africa and Madagascar. It has soft, heart-shaped leaves and attractive red flowers.
Small tree native to Southeast Asia from India to southern China. Its unusual leaves may have a central leaflet surrounded by as many as nine variously lobed leaflets.

A tufted perennial of unstated native origin, found in marshes and seeps on deep sand in South Africa’s Western and Eastern Cape. It has deciduous leaf sheaths and tiny flowers; historically, taller forms near Malmesbury were used for thatching, and the plant also supplied material for brooms and baskets.
A climbing wintergreen flowering plant endemic to the Azores. It has few or no thorns, broad egg-shaped or heart-shaped leaves, and fruits that turn red when ripe.

A perennial, clump-forming sedge found along river and lake margins from northern and central Europe to the lower Volga. It has narrow, flat leaves, three-angled stems and brown flower spikes in late spring and summer.
A sedge native to parts of Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia. It grows in wet places such as river margins and rice fields.
A sedge endemic to southern South Africa, mat sedge grows near rivers and other water reservoirs. It forms tall clumps, and the plant is used for baskets, sleeping mats, twine and other woven goods.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it also occurs across tropical and subtropical regions. It uses C4 photosynthesis, considered exceptional for a European species growing in wet habitats, and occurs in shallow seasonal pools and rice-field weed communities.

Semi-aquatic grass whose native origin is not specified in the supplied information. It has ascending stems from a low base and dark to bluish-green leaves that may be flat or folded. It is considered invasive in some parts of the world.
An annual sedge of unspecified native origin. In Portugal, it grows in temporary ponds and wet depressions, often on siliceous ground that is seasonally flooded or damp.

A rush of the Mediterranean and West Asia, found mainly in wet ground and beside watercourses. Its tubular leaves contain conspicuous crosswise chambers, while its stems may sprawl along the ground; subspecies differ in growth form and fruit shape.
An annual rush, hybrid rush has a self-supporting form and simple, broad leaves.

An annual rush of unstated native origin, it is reliably recorded in Europe and North Asia, though a possibly cosmopolitan range is poorly documented. It is exceptionally small, its flowers rarely open, and it can be easily confused with tiny forms of Juncus bufonius.
A flowering rush distributed across the Mediterranean, Middle East and Central Asia, and introduced to Great Britain. It typically grows in salt marshes.

A flowering sedge native to mainland Portugal and distributed widely worldwide. During the 2016–2019 mainland Portuguese assessment, it was known from one brackish wetland in the eastern Algarve, with no more than 30 mature plants estimated there.

summary: An aquatic flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows mainly in watercourses, rarely in lagoons, and favors alkaline water.
Succulent endemic to South Africa’s Cape Province. It is a low-growing, short-stemmed aloe with small spines that forms dense clusters.

A shrub of unspecified native origin, distributed through South Africa’s Cape provinces in the subtropics. Its small leaves have rolled margins and waxy upper surfaces, while its showy pink flowers appear in autumn.
An evergreen flowering shrub native to Central China. It has spiny leaves, clustered yellow flowers tinged red, and dark purple berries with a white bloom.

A fig tree native to Japan, China, Hong Kong, Taiwan and Southeast Asia as far as Ceram, it can grow from the ground or directly on other trees. Its mature figs vary from whitish pink to dark purple, often with pale spots, and a Taiwanese study found ants living in cavities within young branches.

A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, it occurs around the southern Mediterranean from Algeria to Egypt and Israel, as well as Cyprus, several southern Aegean islands, Sicily and Pantelleria.

A perennial herb native to Switzerland and distributed across temperate Eurasia. It forms dense turf, with stems much shorter than its arching basal leaves, and favors dry rocky places, especially on limestone.

summary: A densely tufted sedge found across Europe and Macaronesia in acidic heathland, woods and grassland. Its rounded female flower spikes sit below a narrower male spike, and ripening seed stalks bend towards the ground, where ants disperse the seeds.

Perennial sedge native to Europe. It has blue-grey leaves, spreads by creeping stems and inhabits sandy marshes, damp dune hollows and coastal heaths in western Europe. In the British Isles it was known only from Ormesby, Norfolk, where it became extinct in 1869.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It has the lowest chromosome number recorded in its genus.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and present in mainland Portugal.

A columnar cactus native to the dry forests of Salta and Jujuy in Argentina, and possibly southern Bolivia. It forms erect, base-branching shoots with many fine whitish spines; its purple-pink flowers open only slightly for one day.

Perennial cactus native to the dry, mountainous cliffsides of Tarija, Bolivia. Its slender upright columns are densely covered with white spines. Older plants produce deep red to burgundy tubular flowers that barely open.

An evergreen climbing herb native from the Mediterranean east to the Urals and Indian subcontinent. It has hairy twining stems and clusters of pink-white flowers; its hanging brown pods contain flattened, winged seeds tipped with silky white hairs.

summary: A flowering cactus native to southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay and northeastern Argentina. Its large, sweet-scented flowers have sharply pointed lavender or white petals, open at night, and may wilt the next afternoon on hot days.

An annual wetland flowering plant of unspecified native origin. In Portugal, it grows on damp or temporarily flooded ground beside freshwater or slightly brackish ponds and lagoons, sometimes occurring in rice fields.

Globose cactus native to Argentina's Catamarca Province. Its flattened, dark grey-green to blue-green body has curved pale-grey spines but no central spines. Red, pink or orange funnel-shaped flowers grow near the top.

A cactus from South America, it grows naturally in Paraguay and northeastern Bolivia. Popular mutants lacking chlorophyll show vivid pink, red, orange or yellow colouring and are usually grafted onto another cactus because they otherwise survive only briefly.

A large, single-stemmed shrub confined to South Africa’s Cape Peninsula, where it grows on damp, rocky southern slopes. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants, and female plants retain winged seeds until fire releases them.

An annual flowering herb endemic to the western Algarve of southern Portugal. Its somewhat fleshy leaves accompany violet flowers marked at the throat with pale yellow and dark violet veins and spots. The small black seeds have fine lengthwise ridges but no wing.

A flowering plant native to Yunnan, Taiwan, the Ryukyu Islands and southwest Japan, Magnolia compressa grows as a small tree in cultivation. It is hardy only to USDA zone 10 and can be grown in containers and brought indoors for winter.
Small evergreen tree or shrub endemic to Madeira. It inhabits woodlands, shrublands and lower-elevation laurel forests, from sea level to 400 metres.
A flowering tree endemic to Bora Bora and Tahiti in French Polynesia’s Society Islands.
Flowering plant endemic to the Madeira Islands, including Madeira and the Desertas. It grows on sea cliffs and rocky offshore islets.

An aquatic waterlily native from Sri Lanka and northeastern India to western and central Malesia, it grows in rivers, lakes and ponds. Its leaves are bronzy red to dark green above and dark purple beneath, while its purplish-red flowers are pleasantly fragrant.
edibilityNote: The flower stalks and seeds are used as food.

summary: An annual, partly parasitic herb endemic to Madeira. It is densely covered with bristly hairs and bears yellow flowers. It grows on wet, often spring-fed rocky slopes in Madeira’s central mountains.
A flowering plant in the carrot family, native only to the Madeira archipelago.
A cactus native to Panama, Colombia, Venezuela and the Caribbean islands. It grows as a dense shrub or tree, with olive-green pads, salmon or pink flowers, and red fruit with edible red flesh.
edibilityNote: The red fruit and its red flesh are edible.

summary: A flowering cactus endemic to Argentina and Bolivia. It usually grows alone but sometimes forms small groups, with rounded reddish-grey to green stems bearing reddish, brown or black central spines and white hairlike outer spines. Its flowers range from yellow through orange to red.
Ball- or cylinder-shaped cactus native to upland southern Brazil and Uruguay. It has a spiny, woolly crown and pale-yellow flowers in summer.

A globular cactus native to Brazil and endemic to Rio Grande do Sul. It usually forms one body but may develop basal stems into compact clumps, with soft, flexible golden-brown spines and pale yellow to golden summer flowers.

A succulent cactus native to northeastern Brazil, recorded in Bahia and Minas Gerais. It grows as a tree-like, many-stemmed clump, distinguished by blue-green stems, golden spines that turn grey, and fruits containing magenta pulp.
A flowering plant endemic to Madeira, Portugal, Plantago malato-belizii is protected under Portuguese or European legislation, including the Habitats Directive.

An annual or perennial aquatic flowering plant found throughout Europe and reaching North Africa and westernmost Asia, brackish water-crowfoot usually grows in slightly salty coastal pools and ditches. It can become terrestrial as its habitat dries in summer. Its white, yellow-based flowers and blue-tipped, usually downward-pointing sepals help distinguish it.
edibilityNote: Explicitly described as not edible.

summary: A flowering plant native to sub-Saharan Africa except West Africa, Madagascar and the Arabian Peninsula, this buttercup grows in wet areas. It is used in traditional medicine for sores and toothaches.

A cactus from South America, found in northern Argentina and Bolivia. Anderson describes clustered globe-shaped stems with fine whitish spines and red flowers arising around the base, while broader treatments include synonyms with yellow to orange flowers.

Shrubby cactus widespread in southern and southeastern Brazil, growing on trees or rocks. Its smooth cylindrical shoots become hanging and richly branched, with yellowish-white flowers followed by flattened, round white fruits.

Shrub or small tree native to parts of the Mediterranean region; plants native to Madeira and the Canary Islands are treated by some as a separate subspecies. It is highly variable, with dark twigs that start hairy and later become smooth, and leaves green above but grey and prominently veined below.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and present in mainland Portugal. It is protected under legislation including Annexes II and IV of the EU Habitats Directive.

A flowering plant endemic to mainland Portugal, especially the western limestone ranges. It commonly grows in rock crevices and other rocky places on limestone, marl or basalt, and can be locally abundant despite its limited range.

An evergreen flowering perennial native to Kenya and Tanzania, the false African violet often bears flowers nearly year-round. Its compact variety has received the Royal Horticultural Society’s Award of Garden Merit as a houseplant.
A flowering plant endemic to Madeira, Portugal, it is protected under Portuguese or European legislation, including Annexes II and IV of the Habitats Directive.

A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it occurs in Portugal only in the Serra da Estrela, around high-altitude springs and stream margins. It is assessed as Vulnerable in mainland Portugal, where only two locations were identified.

summary: A liverwort restricted to Madeira and the Canary Islands. It forms robust, irregularly branched mats ranging from light green to reddish brown, usually on tree bark in laurel forests. It can also grow on shaded rocks and humid soil among leaf litter.
A liverwort endemic to Scotland, northern prongwort is known only from the Beinn Eighe nature reserve. It grows in dwarf shrub heath alongside other large liverworts.
A lily-family plant native to Mediterranean areas of Spain, France, Sardinia, Sicily and Algeria, including the Balearic Islands and Corsica.

An intertidal red alga found along western North America from Baja California to Alaska, it commonly inhabits low-tide pools in moderately exposed or exposed places. South of Monterey Bay, detailed measurements or molecular sequencing may be needed to distinguish it from a similar species.

A marine red alga native to China, Japan, Korea and parts of eastern Russia. Its soft, gelatinous blades range from red to burgundy, becoming yellow when dying or dead, and several blades may arise from one central attachment. It is edible.
edibilityNote: The seaweed is stated to be edible, without details about parts or preparation.

summary: Evergreen climbing plant native to East Asia, including Japan, the Korean Peninsula, the Ryukyu Islands and Taiwan. It clings to trees, cliffs and walls with aerial rootlets, or spreads as ground cover without vertical support. Its leaves are diamond-shaped, and its ripe fruits are black.
edibilityNote: The stems are poisonous if eaten and contain irritating sap.

summary: A shrub native to the western Mediterranean, including southern Iberia, northwestern Africa, the Balearic Islands and the Canary Islands. It typically reaches about one and a half metres, flowers in May and June, sheds its leaves in summer and bears greenish berries.

summary: Annual plant native to several provinces in China and to Taiwan, Japanese purple sage has upright stems and terminal flower clusters. Its flowers range from reddish, purple and blue to white.

A perennial plant found in the eastern and southern Mediterranean Basin, notably Crete. It is an evergreen, woody climber with leathery, deeply heart-shaped leaves and yellow flowers marked with purple stripes and a U-shaped tube.

A small annual herb native in mainland Portugal, within a wider Mediterranean distribution. It grows in rain-fed olive groves on basic clay soils, usually derived from limestone. A 2016–2019 mainland Portuguese assessment classed it as Vulnerable, with intensive agriculture threatening its restricted habitat there.

summary: A usually hairless annual herb whose native origin is not specified. It has somewhat succulent leaves and inconspicuous green flowers; ants disperse its seeds after eating an attached oil-rich body. Young shoots are sometimes eaten as a vegetable.
edibilityNote: Young shoots are sometimes eaten as a vegetable.

summary: A perennial herb native to the Caucasus, including parts of Russia, Armenia and Azerbaijan. It has spreading underground stems, clusters of many lilac flowers and can persist for decades.
A small to medium moss found across the Holarctic and Central America. It forms dense, stiff, shaggy green to brownish mats, with irregularly branching creeping stems and beaked spore capsules.

A terrestrial perennial orchid indigenous in Switzerland and distributed across central and western Europe and the Mediterranean into North Africa. Its white summer flowers form a loose corkscrew-like spike, and it favours wet, calcium-rich, nutrient-poor fens and marshy ground.

summary: A deciduous shrub or small tree native to eastern Asia, from northern and central China through Korea and Japan to southeastern Siberia. It has rounded, often somewhat lobed leaves and bears edible nuts in clusters, partly enclosed by husks.
edibilityNote: The nuts are edible and cultivated commercially in China.

summary: Deciduous shrub native to China, Japan and South Korea. It grows on sunny, forested slopes and has a repeating leaf-angle pattern of 180°, 90°, 180° and 270°.

A small deciduous tree occurring across China, Mongolia, Korea, Siberia and Japan, especially beside streams in wetlands. It resembles the American elm but remains smaller, with a dense, heavily shading canopy and bark that stays smooth for a long time before becoming furrowed.

A deciduous upright shrub found in western Hokkaido and chiefly along Honshu’s Sea of Japan side. It bears trumpet-shaped flowers in May and June that are rose-pink outside and paler within, and is often seen on mountain valley slopes.

A perennial herb native to mainland Portugal, reliably recorded in Trás-os-Montes and Alto Douro. It is an upright, hairy plant with white flowers in small terminal clusters, growing in rock fissures, stony places and rocky floodbeds.

summary: An annual herb native to the Mediterranean region. It is a small, upright or ascending hairy plant with yellow flowers and an inflated, curved pod that is initially fleshy and later leathery.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula. In Portugal’s 2016–2019 assessment, it was known from one adult plant in a single eastern Algarve site, growing in somewhat moist sandy meadow soil.

summary: A perennial herb described as endemic to Madeira’s mountain ranges. It has almost no visible leaves; its branched green stems bear membrane-like wings, and small yellowish-white flower clusters appear in spring and summer. It is used in gaucho mate and to flavour liqueurs and wines.
edibilityNote: Used in gaucho mate and to flavour liqueurs and wines.

summary: A deciduous tree native to Chile and Argentina. Its often-forked trunk has greyish-brown to dark brown bark, and its leaves curl slightly between the veins and toothed edges. Mature trees develop reddish, durable heartwood valued for furniture and construction.

A large perennial flowering herb endemic to the Canary Islands, it has deeply divided leaves in a rosette from a woody base. It can form brilliant carpets on the floors of laurel forests and wax myrtle-tree heath scrub.
An annual or biennial herb native to mainland Portugal. It is characteristic of coastal dunes and sands, occurring mainly along the southern Algarve coast with an isolated population at Troia.

A poisonous perennial herb native to southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa around the Mediterranean, the villous deadly carrot has hairy, divided leaves and bright yellow flower clusters. Its fruits have four wings, while its thick root resembles a white carrot or turnip.
edibilityNote: The plant is described as highly poisonous; its roots can also cause severe itching and swelling on skin contact.

summary: A bristly biennial or perennial herb native to the southern Iberian Peninsula and northwestern Africa. It grows mainly on coastal and near-coastal dunes and sands, and bears blue-grey or blue-violet funnel-shaped flowers.
A liverwort found in Ireland, Germany and the United Kingdom, though the supplied information does not identify these places as its native range.
A moss found globally but almost absent from western North America, Swartz's feather-moss varies greatly in density and leaf shape.

A grass native to much of Europe and parts of southwestern Asia and North Africa. It has elongated underground stems and an open flower cluster, and grows in dry or moist hardwood woodland on deep sandy, rocky or loamy soils.

A moss of unstated native origin, distributed across Europe, Asia and North Africa. It forms loose, shiny green carpets, often with tree-like branching, and has sharply pointed, lengthwise-folded leaves with toothed edges.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. There it grows in meadows and pastures on clay or limestone soils.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A small flowering plant native to the Mediterranean basin. Its stalks have hornlike projections, while the fruit bears a horn covered with curved bristles; it inhabits rock holes, masonry cracks and very dry sand.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual flowering plant represented in mainland Portugal by two varieties, both native there, and distributed more broadly around the Mediterranean. Its fruit is covered with spreading hairs, especially along the ridges, and carries an oblique, clearly net-veined calyx nearly as broad as the fruit.

sources.title: Valerianella eriocarpa Desv.

summary: Violet species whose subspecies Viola alba subsp. alba is native from southern France to southern Poland, northwestern Türkiye and western Syria. That subspecies also has a new record in Kashmir, India.

A flowering plant native to the Iberian Peninsula, Jersey thrift usually has short, tightly clustered branches and dull, narrow, lance-shaped leaves with thin papery edges. Its flower heads have long-pointed outer leaflike parts that extend beyond the middle ones and often the inner ones.
A deciduous shrub native to Korea, Mongolia, Russia and parts of northern China. Its reddish-purple flowers open in late winter or early spring, often on bare branches before the leaves unfold.
edibilityNote: In Korea, the flowers are cooked in traditional spring festival cakes and used in infused liquor.

summary: A flowering plant whose native origin is not securely established by the supplied evidence. It has been reported from coastal cliffs and rocks in Portugal, but herbarium review found no confirmed Portuguese specimens, and its reported occurrence there may reflect confusion with similar species.

A perennial herb in a group containing eight rock sea-lavenders endemic to Britain and Guernsey, it has clusters of small violet-blue flowers. It flourishes in salty soils, especially near western coasts and in salt marshes.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Limonium binervosum
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, found in eastern and central Spain. It has erect stems, leaves with paired leaflets and yellow spring flowers followed by straight fruits containing yellowish-brown seeds.
A flowering plant endemic to Portugal’s Madeira Archipelago, Limonium lowei belongs to the Plumbaginaceae family. It is not protected under Portuguese or European Community legislation.

An annual flowering plant native to the Mediterranean region. Most of the plant is covered with stiff hairs; it bears small yellow flowers and hard, grey-brown fruits divided into four beaked, knobbly nutlets.

sources.title: Neatostema apulum (L.) I.M.Johnst.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual herb of unstated native origin, now recorded across many parts of the world. Its branches spread along the ground, its white flowers form end clusters, and its strongly curved fruits resemble fishing hooks.
An annual herb native to the Canary Islands. It has narrow, pointed leaves with parallel veins and nearly round, finely bumpy fruits whose ribs are barely visible.

A mat-forming annual native to North Africa, Europe and Asia, prostrate spurge has small greyish leaves that may be weakly toothed or toothless. Its fruits may be hairy or hairless, while tiny white or pinkish structures surrounding yellowish or reddish floral glands create the flower-like display.

A perennial bulb-forming herb native throughout the Mediterranean basin. Its fragrant ivory-white flowers surround a glossy dark ovary and yellow anthers. All parts are highly toxic, especially the bulb.
edibilityNote: All parts, especially the bulb, contain highly toxic compounds and are poisonous if ingested.

sources.title: Ornithogalum arabicum L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual hairy herb occurring in North Africa, western Asia and southern Europe. It has branched upright or rising stems, serrated rounded leaflets and small pink flower heads, blooming from May to June.

A perennial plant found in southern and central Europe. It is distinguished by a round black berry enclosed by the persistent flower cup, along with pointed oval leaves and pale yellowish-white flowers.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It parasitizes herbaceous legumes and bears dark-purple hairy, glandular stems with spikes of dark reddish-purple flowers.

An evergreen perennial herb native across the Iberian Peninsula, Balearic Islands, France, Italy, Malta and North Africa. Its solitary flower heads have overlapping bracts whose broad, spoon-like tips create a pinecone appearance, surrounding white to pink florets that often have purple tips.
Annual herb with no native origin stated in the supplied source. It is self-supporting, has simple leaves and remains very small.

A small evergreen shrub native to Europe’s western Mediterranean region, Cneorum tricoccon has a nearly rounded form. Its yellowish flowers appear from June to July, followed by seeds ripening from August to September.
edibilityNote: Its fruit is described as having no food value, but not explicitly as inedible.

summary: A flowering plant native to southeastern Europe, including parts of Italy, Greece, Albania and the former Yugoslavia.
An evergreen tree native to Japan and the Ryukyu Islands. Its nuts are edible but bitter and contain tannins, which soaking in water removes; it is also cultivated as an ornamental.
edibilityNote: The bitter nuts are edible for people; soaking them in water removes their tannins.

summary: Ornamental shrub native from central China to the Korean Peninsula. It flowers in May and bears small, sour fruit reported to have a pleasantly sweet flavour and to be used in pies.
edibilityNote: The fruit is reported to be sweet but sour and used in pies.

summary: A plant native to China, Mallotus japonicus is also found in Japan and Korea. It has red young shoots and large leaves traditionally used to wrap food; its young leaves are edible when boiled.
edibilityNote: Young leaves are edible when boiled; large leaves were traditionally used to wrap food.

summary: A flowering grass native to Europe and Asia. It was deliberately planted in North America and now occurs in several US states.
A tree in the olive family, with no native origin stated in the supplied text. Its toothed oval leaves are dark green above and dark blue beneath, with both surfaces hairless.

A shrub native to South Africa, the limestone pincushion grows in coastal fynbos on limestone deposits. Its globe-shaped flower heads are usually grouped in twos or threes, with bright yellow flowers that turn orange over time. Flowering occurs between August and December.

A tropical strangler tree native to Southeast Asia and Northeast Australia, it begins on a larger tree and eventually engulfs it. Dense woolly hairs, greyish-white bark and bright yellow-to-red fleshy fruit distinguish it.

A wood-sorrel-family plant native to Central America and western South America, spiral woodsorrel is cultivated ornamentally. Its cultivars include foliage ranging from bright yellow-green and copper-red to nearly black or variegated purple.

An endangered tree fern of mountain rainforests in East and Southeast Asia. In Japan, its new leaves and shoots are boiled to remove bitterness before being eaten, while its boiled core is a festival food on the Yaeyama and Ishigaki islands.
edibilityNote: Stem starch is eaten in China and Taiwan; Japan uses boiled young leaves and shoots, and boiled core as a regional festival food.

summary: A succulent shrub native to South Africa’s Western Cape, Eastern Cape and southern KwaZulu-Natal, it grows on dry, rocky ground. Its rounded, powdery gray leaves have red edges and resemble silver dollars, while star-shaped pink or white flowers appear in summer.

Plant occurring in two widely separated areas: the mountains of southern France and north-central and eastern Spain, and the Baltic islands of Öland and Gotland. It lacks runners, and its flower cup has teeth about as long as its tube.

An aromatic perennial shrub endemic to the Madeira archipelago, it grows on rocky coastal sites in Madeira and the Desertas and is common around Porto Santo’s peaks and islets. It has whitish-grey felted growth, triangular leaves and dense clusters of small yellow-centred flower heads.
Plant endemic to the Canary Islands, frequent in dry areas at lower elevations. It has rounded flower heads and flat leaf lobes.

A salt-tolerant shrub distributed across parts of Africa, the Middle East and eastward to India, with no specific native origin stated. Its woody-based, heavily branched growth occurs naturally in salt-affected habitats, including coastal bushland, saline inland sites, desert wadis and dry riverbeds.

A moss of unspecified native origin, it is widespread in Europe and reported from nearby parts of Africa and Asia. Its broad, dull-green leaves have a nerve that stops short of the tip, and it rarely produces spores, usually dispersing through small orange gemmae.
A liverwort native to Eurasia and North America, it is a short-lived terrestrial plant associated with pioneer vegetation.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Bulbous flowering perennial native to South Africa, specifically the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State and Drakensberg Mountains. It bears faintly scented, bright pink flowers with frilly tips in late summer and autumn, while its strap-shaped leaves do not appear until spring.

A creeping flowering shrub native to rocky slopes in Tibet, Sichuan and Yunnan in China. It is drought-tolerant and has small glossy leaves, tiny rose-like flowers and showy red fruit; its low growth also suits bonsai.

A deciduous shrub native to central and eastern Europe and southwest Asia; Spanish plants may also belong to this species. Its leaves have pale grey hairs underneath, while its small white or pale pink flowers are followed by dark red fruits.
A plant species found on Atlantic Forest hillsides in Paraná and Santa Catarina, Brazil. It grows 4–6 metres tall, but can reach 30 metres in cultivation, and fruits from January to March.
Flowering plant endemic to the Canary Islands. It forms large leaf rosettes close to the ground, with tall spikes of yellow flowers; its five subspecies are native to different islands.

An evergreen climbing shrub native to western Iberia and northern Morocco. Its aerial rootlets cling to trees, cliffs and walls, while unsupported plants form ground cover; it has broad leathery leaves and black ripe fruits.

A deciduous tree native to the Caspian region of northern Iran and southeastern Azerbaijan. Its smooth bark peels into a patchwork of pink, cinnamon, green and pale yellow, while its glossy leaves turn purple, orange and brilliant red in autumn.

Orchid native to Peru, Bolivia and Brazil, mainly found in very wet, moss-covered, semi-boggy areas. Its fragrant flowers are green with red-brown markings and have a white lip marked with violet. Successfully pollinated flowers close slightly and may remain colourful for up to three months.

Coastal succulent occurring along western South Africa from around Cape Town and the Cape Peninsula east to Mossel Bay. Numerous serpent-like stems arise from a short central base, giving it the appearance of Medusa's head.

A flowering plant native to Bangladesh, Thailand, Laos, Vietnam and southeastern and south-central China, where it inhabits tropical swamps and rainforests. It has lance-shaped leaves growing from a central point and occasionally produces white flowers followed by oval reddish fruits. Its calcium oxalate crystals are poisonous if ingested and can severely burn and swell the mouth and tongue.
edibilityNote: Calcium oxalate crystals make the plant poisonous if ingested, causing severe burning and swelling of the mouth and tongue.

summary: A small deciduous tree native to China, Taiwan, Myanmar, Laos and Vietnam. It bears white flowers in early spring and variably coloured plums; fully ripe fruit can be eaten raw, while the pits and leaves are poisonous to humans.
edibilityNote: Fully ripe fruit can be eaten raw; pits and leaves are poisonous, with crushed pits especially advised against.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to Colombia. It occurs in the departments of Antioquia, Boyacá, Cundinamarca, Meta and Santander.

A tree found across the Indian subcontinent, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, usually beside rivers or dry riverbeds. It has a buttressed trunk, broad crown, smooth grey bark and fibrous, five-winged fruit. Its leaves feed the moth that produces commercially important wild tassar silk.

An annual flowering legume native to mainland Portugal, it grows there in mountain meadows and woods, as well as on rocky ground and cliffs, generally on stony soils. It has a wider Mediterranean and Macaronesian distribution but is sparsely recorded and assessed as Near Threatened in mainland Portugal.

sources.attribution: Info Flora, plazi (2021). Info Flora Schweiz - Fabaceae. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/wwu2n2 accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A sub-shrub and herb native to the western Mediterranean region, felty germander has small pink-to-white flowers. Its leaves are used in cooking and medicine, although the plant may cause liver toxicity.
edibilityNote: Leaves are used in cooking; the plant also has traditional medicinal use and potential liver toxicity.

summary: A flowering plant native to Bolivia, southern Brazil, northern Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay. Widely introduced through drier tropical and subtropical regions, it has escaped gardens and become an environmental weed in parts of Australia.

Bromeliad naturally found in Atlantic Coast restinga vegetation from Bahia to Espírito Santo in eastern Brazil. It forms many long, thorny leaves and may be orange, green, crimson or yellow. It usually grows on the ground but can also grow on other plants.

A subtropical succulent native to the arid Karoo of South Africa’s Eastern Cape, Euphorbia obesa is a thornless, ball-shaped plant. It usually has eight ridges and grey-green skin marked with lighter or darker horizontal stripes, sometimes developing red and purple areas in direct sunlight. Its latex is toxic.
A climbing wintergreen flowering plant occurring in Madeira and the Canary Islands. It has few or no thorns, simple flower clusters and fruits that turn black when ripe.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it has narrow, hairy leaves and an upright cylindrical flower spike. In Portugal it grows in sparse annual grasslands, banks and clearings, especially in dry, exposed and somewhat nitrogen-rich places.
