summary: A densely foliaged shrub or small tree native to Australia, moonah has rough dark bark and a trunk often twisted by wind. Its white or cream flower spikes appear mainly in summer, followed by woody capsules spaced along the branches.
A geophyte occurring in KwaZulu-Natal, from the Ngome Forests to the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands. It has fewer than ten subpopulations and has lost 30% of its habitat in the past 90 years.
Flowering plant whose subspecies Silene psammitis subsp. psammitis is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and occurs in mainland Portugal.
Flowering plant whose listed varieties, var. nitida and var. meridionalis, are native to mainland Portugal.

A large shrub or small tree endemic to southern and eastern South Africa and neighbouring territories such as Eswatini, it bears abundant, extremely fragrant flowers with long tubes accessible only to nocturnal hawkmoths. Its hard, woody fruit can remain on the tree for years if large browsers or elephants do not eat it.
An asphodel endemic to the Iberian Peninsula.
A flowering shrub native to South America, shell flower grows in shady, damp places and has yellow flowers.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and the Madeira Archipelago, belonging to the pea family.

Small herbaceous plant of unspecified native origin, found in the central and southern Iberian Peninsula. It has hairy reddish, usually unbranched upright stems and vivid yellow flower heads in spring; its seeds bear tufts for wind dispersal.

An Iberian-endemic herbaceous perennial, Leucanthemopsis pallida is usually covered in whitish hairs and woody at the base. Its outer flowers may be yellow or white; above 1,700 metres they are white, often tinged with purple.
A flowering plant whose subspecies Ranunculus ollissiponensis subsp. ollissiponensis is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and occurs in mainland Portugal.
Flowering plant with no explicitly stated native origin for the species; its Madeira subspecies is endemic to Macaronesia.

A low shrub or small tree native to the Canary Islands, western Morocco and Western Sahara. Its spineless, partly succulent stems carry leaves clustered at their tips. In the Canary Islands, the leaves were gathered and cooked as greens, while its milky latex is poisonous.
edibilityNote: In the Canary Islands, leaves were historically gathered and cooked as a green vegetable; the milky latex is poisonous.

summary: A shrub endemic to Macaronesia, occurring on some Canary Islands and Madeira. It is distinguished by hanging flower clusters, divided leaves with oval leaflets, and pear-shaped fruits.
Perennial flowering plant endemic to La Palma in the Canary Islands. Its many flower heads have pink outer flowers and mauve-purple centres, accompanied by roughly rounded, toothed leaves.

A climbing groundcover native to Australia, climbing saltbush spreads in vine-like, light-green branches with small, semi-succulent arrowhead leaves. Its inconspicuous green summer flowers become conspicuous tiny bright-red berries in early autumn. Early European settlers around Adelaide boiled it with other saltbushes as a substitute for greens.
edibilityNote: Early European settlers around Adelaide boiled the plant with other saltbush species as a substitute for greens.

summary: A flowering shrub endemic to La Palma in the Canary Islands. It normally produces numerous spikes of blue flowers in early summer, although a hybrid may have white or pink flowers, and it tolerates cold poorly.
Flowering plant native to the western Mediterranean. Its tissues contain the diterpenoid alkaloid graciline.

Germander endemic to southwestern Portugal, it is restricted to the Southwest Alentejo and Vicentine Coast Natural Park. It grows in low scrubland on fixed dunes, cliffs and coastal rocks, on sand or limestone.

A small shrub native to France, Spain and the Mediterranean, it grows in sandy ground around beaches. Its white flowers are tinged purple and bloom in March and April; in mainland Portugal it is restricted to limestone sea cliffs in the southwestern Algarve.

summary: A perennial herb endemic to the western Mediterranean, the shrubby violet blooms throughout winter and into early spring. Its flowers naturally occur in colours including magenta, gold, blue, purple, maroon and off-white.

summary: A shrub endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula, in southern Portugal and southwestern Spain. Usually low-growing, it has narrow dark-green leaves and white flowers with a yellow spot at each petal’s base.

An annual thistle native to the Mediterranean region and Middle East, with deeply lobed, grey-green leaves marked by white veins. Sharp spines edge the leaves and surround its dense purple flower heads.
edibilityNote: On Crete, tender shoots are peeled and eaten raw.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula.
A flowering plant in the mint family whose subspecies Micromeria graeca subsp. graeca is native to mainland Portugal.
A flowering plant native to continental Portugal.
A flowering plant native to Spain, including the Balearic Islands, France, including Corsica, Portugal and Sardinia. It belongs to the lily family.
A slow-growing shrub native to southern Africa, it has solitary reddish flowers, often bright red in Richtersveld. Its seeds develop inside distinctive inflated capsules resembling Chinese lanterns.

A flowering plant found in southern Spain and parts of North Africa, growing among rocks and at the foot of rocky slopes. It has thick, hairy, heart-shaped leaves and pink flowers crowded towards the tops of its flower spikes.
A perennial or biennial herb endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It has tall glandular-hairy stems, deeply lobed leaves and solitary yellow flowers marked dark purple at the base.

A moss with no native origin stated, dwarf neckera occurs in much of Europe, southwest Asia, North Africa, the Canary Islands and Madeira. It forms slightly glossy green mats and often bears threadlike shoots used for vegetative reproduction. It usually grows on tree bark in shady, humid forests, but occasionally occurs on rocks or old walls.
Flowering plant represented in mainland Portugal by three varieties described as native there.
An ornamental sedge native to central and southern Japan. Its many cultivars are mostly variegated, and it tolerates heavy shade and wet soil while spreading slowly as ground cover.

A planktonic green microalga found in temperate or tropical nutrient-poor lakes and estuaries; no native origin is stated. Its colonies sit in a lipid-rich matrix, and much of its hydrocarbon oil lies outside its thick-walled cells.
edibilityNote: Its hydrocarbon oils are described as inedible.

summary: Evergreen succulent perennial native to the southern Alps in Europe. It forms rosettes of thick, water-storing leaves, usually green with reddish-purple tips, and reproduces both by budding and by flowering once before dying.

A unicellular desmid found worldwide in acidic waters, especially around the edges of large ponds and lakes. Its symmetrical cell is deeply divided into two identical halves, whose corners extend into paired straight or slightly curved spines.
An evergreen shrub endemic to Brazil, becoming semi-deciduous in cooler areas. Its non-fragrant flowers open pale purple and fade to white.

A flowering plant whose subspecies globulariifolia is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and occurs in mainland Portugal. The variety major is likewise Iberian-endemic and present in mainland Portugal, where it has legal protection under European conservation measures.
A prostrate shrub native to Spain and Portugal.

Perennial herb endemic to the southwestern coastal strip of the Iberian Peninsula. In mainland Portugal it grows in sandy scrub and open pinewoods between Olhão and the São Vicente plateau; assessments conducted in 2016–2019 classified it as Vulnerable because of its limited range and declining habitat and mature population.

summary: Wild onion native to Spain, Portugal, Morocco and Algeria in the western Mediterranean.

A perennial wild onion native to parts of the Mediterranean, including southern Europe, North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean. It bears tight flower clusters with white tepals that may have pink or red midveins.
A flowering plant in the pea family, native to mainland Portugal and introduced to Madeira.
A flowering plant originating in Central Asia that produces apples. It has been introduced to mainland Portugal and the Azores.

A succulent shrub whose native origin is not stated, it has grey-green shoots and broad, simple leaves. Its daisy-like flowers have yellow centres and petals that vary between pink and purple with the season.
A rainforest tree endemic to eastern Australia. It has narrow, glossy leaves and end-of-branch clusters of white flowers, followed by spherical red berries with white flesh surrounding one seed.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it grows in sparse grassland and openings in dry scrub or pine woods. It favours sandy, acidic soils.

summary: Woody flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and introduced in the Azores. A 1913 account describes lance-shaped leaves and stems that become almost leafless, with flowering from July to November. It occurred mainly in central and southern cultivated ground, hedges, paths and coastal sands.

Perennial bulbous herb native to the western Mediterranean, including central and southern Portugal, Spain and North Africa. Its narrow green leaves have a white stripe that tends to fade during flowering, while its flowers are white inside with a broad green stripe outside.
A unicellular green alga with a cosmopolitan distribution. It lives in fresh water across a wide range of acidity and alkalinity.

A compact, highly branched shrub of unspecified native origin, it grows in rock crevices in South Africa. It has grey, hairy twigs, tightly rolled needle-shaped leaves and dense heads of small white flowers.
An evergreen shrub or small tree native to South Africa. Its reddish, bare twigs carry leathery leaves with differently coloured surfaces, while its small fragrant flowers are white and purple.

A freshwater green alga with a cosmopolitan distribution, Gonium pectorale usually forms colonies of 16 cells, though colonies may have 8 or 32. Its typical colony has four central cells surrounded by 12 cells with their flagella pointing outward.

An aromatic, deciduous spiny shrub native to parts of East and Southeast Asia and the northern Indian subcontinent. Its fruit and seeds provide timut pepper, valued in Nepalese cooking for its aroma and numbing sensation, while winged leaf stalks help distinguish the plant.
edibilityNote: Fruit and seeds are used as timut pepper; in Nepal they season sauces, pickles, meats, dumplings and other dishes.

summary: A herbaceous perennial native to Mexico. Its dark red to brownish-red flowers smell like chocolate, with the fragrance becoming stronger toward the end of the day, but the plant should not be eaten.
edibilityNote: The plant is explicitly described as unsuitable for eating despite its chocolate-like scent.

summary: A cactus with an uncertain native range because sources disagree. It has been introduced to regions across the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Madagascar and eastern Australia.

A low, shrubby thistle native to Madeira and the Canary Islands, growing on cliffs and rocky slopes. Its narrow, leathery leaves have densely white-felted undersides, and its flower heads contain creamy-yellow tubular florets surrounded by stiff bracts.
A flowering plant in the daisy family, native only to the Madeira archipelago.
A low-growing plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it occurs in perennial grasslands on acidic ground. Its habitats include mountains, Atlantic-influenced sites and coastal cliffs.
A cactus of unspecified native origin. After its spines are removed, the fruit is eaten raw or stewed, dried for winter, or ground into flour for mush by the Zuni people.
edibilityNote: The Zuni remove fruit spines, then eat the fruit raw or stewed, dry it, or grind it into flour for mush.

summary: A moss whose native origin is not stated, recorded in Europe, North Africa, the Azores, the Canary Islands and North America. It usually forms loose mats on deciduous trees, with creeping main shoots and short upright branches. Its capsules sit on short side shoots and are partly enclosed by elongated leaves.

Rare subtropical rainforest tree of unspecified native origin, occurring on volcanic soils around the Mount Warning area of eastern Australia. It has unusually large, thick leaves; its pale fruit is unpleasant raw but valued in mixed preserves.
edibilityNote: The fruit is unpleasant raw but described as an excellent ingredient in mixed preserves.

summary: Fern native to Madeira and Africa from Kenya to South Africa, occurring in subtropical regions.
A shrub native to mainland Portugal, it grows in heathland, scrub and openings in cork-oak or holm-oak woods. It favours acidic soils and sometimes occurs on coastal sands and cliffs.

summary: Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. Its wider range is limited to southwestern Iberia, northwestern Morocco and the Canary Islands, where it inhabits saline margins of small coastal brackish lagoons that dry in summer. In mainland Portugal it is currently known only from the southern Algarve coast.

summary: A flowering shrub native to Eswatini, KwaZulu-Natal and South Africa's Cape Provinces. It is known as the sweet pea shrub and is considered of least ecological concern in South Africa.

A small deciduous tree or shrub native to northeastern China, Korea and the Russian Far East, it has lobed leaves that turn red, yellow and orange in autumn and may remain dried on the plant through winter. New growth bears white, sticky hairs, distinguishing it from the similar Acer sieboldianum.

A shrub found in the Western Ghats’ shola forests in Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Its purplish-blue flowers appear in September and October on a documented 12-year cycle; each individual reproduces once and then dies.

A Kalanchoe species native to Madagascar, Kalanchoe porphyrocalyx has produced many cultivars. The many-flowered cultivar ‘Wendy’ may come from this species alone or from a cross with Kalanchoe miniata.
A small to medium-sized tree, Chinese hawthorn has bright red fruit; its native origin is not stated. In northern Chinese cuisine, the ripe fruit is used in desserts, sweets, preserves and wine.
edibilityNote: Ripe fruits are used in northern Chinese desserts and traditionally in candies, preserves, wine and Cantonese sweet-and-sour sauce.

summary: A wild rose native to Mediterranean Europe, it occurs from the Iberian Peninsula and southern France to parts of Italy and the larger western Mediterranean islands.

Perennial flowering plant native to temperate Eurasia, from Europe to Siberia and parts of western, central and eastern Asia. It can grow from underground stems, and its three accepted subspecies have distinct geographic ranges.

A perennial herb native to Malta, Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, southern Italy and Spain. It is deep-rooted and drought-resistant, with red flowers and jointed pods whose thorny yellow surface turns brown when mature.
A perennial flowering plant native to South Africa’s Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal, as well as Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania and Zambia.
A small, variable succulent native to South Africa’s Western Cape Province. It usually has sharp triangular leaves with channels, keels and faint striped bands of spots, and it can form dense clumps.

A corm-forming flowering plant, Biarum tenuifolium has six generally recognised subspecies distributed from Portugal and Spain through the central Mediterranean to Turkey and Crete. Two Iberian subspecies are associated respectively with heavy terra rossa and loose sandy soils.

A creeping perennial herb endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, Biarum mendax is restricted to the southwest and, in Portugal, to inland Alentejo. It grows on basic, non-calcareous soils along road embankments and traditional rain-fed olive groves. A 2020 mainland Portugal assessment, based on work in 2016–2019, classified it as Endangered amid continuing population and habitat decline.

summary: Flowering plant native to the rainforest of southern Brazil. It forms rosettes of strap-shaped leaves with red tips and red inner leaves, producing blue flowers with red or purple bracts in summer.

A charophyte green alga native to Europe and now widespread worldwide, fragile stonewort inhabits fresh and brackish water. Its originally documented form has short end segments and a black, finely textured fossa wall.
A succulent subshrub native to the southwestern Cape Province, growing mainly in the subtropical biome.

summary: A cactus-like shrub native to North Africa, Euphorbia officinarum has upright, branched stems with five to ten angles, strong paired spines and leaves reduced to tiny bumps. Its flowers range from yellow to red-purple depending on the subspecies.

Flowering plant indigenous to South Africa, where it occurs sparingly around Uitenhage, Patensie and north of Port Elizabeth. It typically lacks leaf blades, and its flower clusters remain shorter than its leaves.
A tropical ground-cover plant native to Brazil. Its pale-green oval leaves have alternating fishbone-like stripes and tend to close at night.

Ground-dwelling orchid native to the western Mediterranean. During the 2016–2019 mainland Portugal assessment, only 72 mature plants were counted across two separated woodland populations, leading to an Endangered assessment.

summary: Perennial herb native to Australian coastal areas and saline flats. It may lie flat or grow upright, and bears green flowers during October and November in its native range.

A medium-sized fern native to the Americas, it typically grows on dry, rocky slopes. Its clustered fronds do not unfurl as fiddleheads, and its unusually little-divided leaflets have golden hairs above and dense white-to-rusty hairs below.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, mountain parsley has a wider European distribution but in Portugal occurs only in the highlands of northeastern Trás-os-Montes, along woodland edges and in clearings. In the 2016–2019 mainland Portugal assessment, it was considered Vulnerable, with only three known locations and a small occupied area, although its national population was then regarded as stable.

summary: A flowering plant native to Bermuda, Bermudiana has strap-like green to grey-green leaves. In spring it bears groups of purple-blue flowers with yellow centres, followed by dark pods containing many small black seeds.
